soil_archetypes.name: Thin Stony Loam
soil_archetypes.description: A shallow, gritty mountain terrace loam crowded with sharp angular shale and granite fragments. It ranges from a pale greyish-brown to dull umber. It feels gritty and loose between the fingers, rarely clumping together, and hits solid rock ledge within one hand's depth.

hand_tests.procedure: Scoop a handful of slightly damp soil from one knuckle deep, squeeze it firmly into a fist for the count of three breaths, then open the palm and poke the lump gently with one finger.
hand_tests.interpretation: If the ball holds shape firmly like dough, clay is adequate; if it crumbles into loose gravel and dust upon the lightest touch, the soil is excessively stony and starved of humus, meaning water will drain away faster than roots can drink.

hand_tests.procedure: Plunge a straight, dried pine stick as thick as your thumb straight down into the bed with steady palm pressure until it stops.
hand_tests.interpretation: If the stick penetrates deeper than your wrist, the soil pocket can host taproots; if it hits hard shelf before reaching your mid-palm, root space is critically shallow and requires mounding or bed raising.

hand_tests.procedure: Drop two handfuls of soil into an old food jar or wide neck bottle, fill with stream water, shake vigorously while singing a short work song, then set on a flat slate for one candle-flicker of time.
hand_tests.interpretation: Heavy stones and sand drop to the bottom instantly; loam settles as a thin middle layer; if the water above remains clear with barely a fingernail-thickness of dark organic scum floating on top, the soil is starved of organic matter.

hand_tests.procedure: Dig up a handful of earth from root level, cup it in both hands, warm it with three deep exhalations, and inhale deeply through the nose.
hand_tests.interpretation: A sweet, rich smell like fallen autumn woods indicates living healthy earth; a sharp vinegar tang or dead metallic stench indicates sour, water-starved, or oxygen-choked soil requiring wood ash and airing.

hand_tests.procedure: Dig a hole one hand's span wide and one hand's depth deep, spread the excavated soil across a flat slate, and count every living wriggler or grub.
hand_tests.interpretation: Finding three or more active earthworms means the biological engine is alive; zero worms means the terrace is sterile, excessively cold, or too acidic, demanding immediate dung and leaf mould infusions.

dominant_failures: Rapid drought from wind desiccation and hyper-fast drainage
Stone volume exceeding half the bed capacity, crowding out root expansion
Severe nutrient leaching during fierce spring snowmelt torrents
Shallow root anchorage causing plants to topple under fierce mountain gales

remediation_steps.action: Surface Stone Sieving and Border Raking
remediation_steps.materials: Pitted wooden laths or interlaced willow sieve, hands, wooden rake
remediation_steps.amount: Two large bucketfuls of stone chips removed per pace length
remediation_steps.purpose: Clears root runways so taproots do not deform or split against jagged granite chips.

remediation_steps.materials: Crumbled dark leaf duff gathered from sheltered cliff hollows and rotted pine needle mould
remediation_steps.amount: Four generous double-handfuls worked into every pace of planting bed
remediation_steps.purpose: Creates moisture-holding spongy pockets that prevent midday mountain winds from baking the root zone dry.

remediation_steps.materials: Grey powdery ash collected from hardwood and seasoned conifer hearth fires
remediation_steps.amount: One level handful scattered evenly across each pace of planting trench
remediation_steps.purpose: Tames the sour runoff washed down from highland scree and releases locked earth minerals.

remediation_steps.materials: Crushed black campfire charcoal pulverized to pea-sized bits and quenched in animal dung tea
remediation_steps.amount: Two handfuls blended with topsoil around each seedling station
remediation_steps.purpose: Acts as permanent microporous micro-batteries for water and beneficial microbes in thin ground.

soil_archetypes.name: Gravelly Mountain Scree
soil_archetypes.description: Loose, rattling slope-wash consisting of fingernail to palm-sized jagged slate and schist fragments bound with meager coarse grit. It lacks cohesive earth, feels dry and raspy, and offers zero resistance to a thrusting boot heel.

hand_tests.procedure: Drive your boot heel sharply down into the surface and twist half a circle.
hand_tests.interpretation: If the ground rattles loose and rolls away like dry peas, it will wash down the mountain during the first rainstorm unless anchored with wattling.

hand_tests.procedure: Rub a pinch of moist scree fines between your thumb and index finger next to your ear.
hand_tests.interpretation: A loud grating scratch with no greasy slip confirms nearly pure mineral stone dust with zero clay binder.

hand_tests.procedure: Place a bare palm flat on the scree stones at high noon, then return and touch it three hand-breadths after sunset.
hand_tests.interpretation: If scorching hot at midday but bone-numbingly cold by twilight, the bed experiences wild thermal swings that will shock young roots without thick organic capping.

hand_tests.procedure: Tip half a bucketful of water onto the scree from knee height.
hand_tests.interpretation: If the water vanishes instantly with a hiss leaving the top stones dry within twenty paces of walking, water holding is zero.

hand_tests.procedure: Swirl a handful of fine scree dust in a drinking horn or cup of water and let stand.
hand_tests.interpretation: If sediment drops like lead shot leaving crystal clear water with no murkiness, there are zero colloidal clays to bind nutrients.

dominant_failures: Absolute inability to store water between mountain showers
Extreme temperature swings from blistered rock noon to freezing night
Physical creep and downhill drift during rainstorms
Severe nutrient starvation with no clay or humus buffer

remediation_steps.materials: Flexible green willow and hazel wands driven across the contour
remediation_steps.amount: One woven barrier one shin-height tall every three paces down the terrace
remediation_steps.purpose: Stabilizes rolling scree and catches downward-drifting silt.

remediation_steps.materials: Heavy clay dug from mountain seepages whipped with stream water in a bucket
remediation_steps.amount: Three bucketfuls poured directly into the stone gravel bed per pace
remediation_steps.purpose: Plugs cavernous voids between scree rocks, providing an adhesive matrix that stops water from plunging straight to bedrock.

remediation_steps.materials: Thick wild pasture sod sliced from native mountain grass tussocks
remediation_steps.amount: One turf layer laid grass-side-down over the grouted scree across the whole bed
remediation_steps.purpose: Forms a rotting fibrous blanket that holds moisture and creates a biological growing floor.

remediation_steps.materials: Overwintered straw and dung scraped from shelter corners
remediation_steps.amount: A blanket spread as thick as four fingers across the bed
remediation_steps.purpose: Insulates against wild temperature fluctuations and feeds decomposing soil fungi.

soil_archetypes.name: Compacted Glacial Clay Pocket
soil_archetypes.description: Dense, cold, blue-grey or dull ochre clay trapped in terrace hollows or near bedrock seepage. It feels greasy and heavy when wet, rolling into slick ribbons, but sets into brick-hard crusts that fissure with deep cracks under drying winds.

hand_tests.procedure: Take a walnut-sized ball of wet soil, roll it between your palms into a thumb-thick snake, and push it over your forefinger until it snaps of its own weight.
hand_tests.interpretation: If the ribbon extends past two finger knuckles before breaking, the earth is dense, heavy clay that will suffocate roots if not opened with grit and fluff.

hand_tests.procedure: Moisten a thumbnail-sized patch of clay with spit and rub it firmly with the ball of your thumb.
hand_tests.interpretation: If it shines like polished shoe leather without scratching, fine colloidal clay dominates, which blocks water infiltration when dry.

hand_tests.procedure: Scoop out a hole the size of your two fists, pour in a bowl of water, and watch the time it takes to sink away.
hand_tests.interpretation: If water sits stagnant for longer than it takes to boil a survival stew over campfire, root rot and suffocating stagnation are certain during cold spells.

hand_tests.procedure: Dig down a forearm's depth into the clay bed and immediately sniff the freshly severed clod.
hand_tests.interpretation: A smell of rotten ditch swamp or sour bog indicates dead, anaerobic ground lacking air; sweet earth smell indicates living pore channels.

hand_tests.procedure: Take an egg-sized clod dried in the sun and attempt to crush it between your thumb and fingers.
hand_tests.interpretation: If it resists all finger pressure and requires a rock hammer blow to shatter, it will strangle seedling emergence without heavy winter frost-flaking.

dominant_failures: Waterlogging and total oxygen starvation in root zones
Slowest to warm up in spring, lagging behind other beds by up to a full moon cycle
Heaving viciously during hard frosts, snapping brittle plant roots
Rock-hard surface crusting preventing seedling emergence

remediation_steps.action: Coarse River Sand and Fine Gravel Incorporation
remediation_steps.materials: Coarse gritty sand washed clean by mountain stream rapids
remediation_steps.amount: Three generous bucketfuls worked into every pace length
remediation_steps.purpose: Fractures the dense clay matrix with permanent non-collapsible drainage pores.

remediation_steps.materials: Heavy digging spade or sturdy sharpened fire-hardened wooden stake
remediation_steps.amount: Tossed into knee-high jagged ridges before the first hard winter freeze
remediation_steps.purpose: Allows ice needles to expand within clods, naturally pulverizing the stubborn clay into fine crumbly tilth.

remediation_steps.action: Crushed Dry Bracken and Chaff Blending
remediation_steps.materials: Crisp dried mountain bracken fern, shredded conifer bark, and crushed dry brush
remediation_steps.amount: Two armfuls per pace buried deep into trench bottoms
remediation_steps.purpose: Keeps the subsoil porous and stops clay from recombining into a solid slick mass.

remediation_steps.materials: Fine wood ash from cold campfire ash pits
remediation_steps.amount: Two handfuls dusted over each pace of raised ridge
remediation_steps.purpose: Flakes clay colloids together into looser crumbs while counteracting sour wet stagnation.

soil_archetypes.name: Coarse Granite Sand Shelf
soil_archetypes.description: Pale buff to sparkling white decomposed granite sand resting on sheltered terrace steps. Highly abrasive, gritty, completely devoid of stickiness, and lets water pour through as freely as dry seeds through fingers.

hand_tests.procedure: Plunge both hands into the damp sand, compress into a tight snowball shape, and release onto a flat rock.
hand_tests.interpretation: If the mound immediately slumps into a flat heap like beach sand, organic binding agents are absent and nutrients will wash away on the next shower.

hand_tests.procedure: Rub a damp handful vigorously into your open palm and blow the sand away.
hand_tests.interpretation: If your skin remains clean and unsoiled without a dark brown earthy smudge, the sand is completely barren of vital humus.

hand_tests.procedure: Kneel close to the bed on a dry windy morning and blow gently across the dry surface.
hand_tests.interpretation: If the sand lifts into a flying blinding spray, seedling roots will be stripped bare by mountain winds unless anchored with a heavy top mulch.

hand_tests.procedure: Push your index finger straight down into the bed with no digging motion.
hand_tests.interpretation: If your finger sinks to the palm with zero effort, soil is wonderfully loose for root growth but structurally unstable against mountain downpours.

hand_tests.procedure: Thoroughly wet a patch at sunrise and touch it again when the sun reaches three hand-breadths above the mountain ridge.
hand_tests.interpretation: If the surface feels dry and warm as dust already, moisture retention is critically deficient.

dominant_failures: Inability to hold water in the upper root zone
Wind scouring stripping fine roots bare during gusty dry spells
Nutrient emptiness, causing seedling yellowing and stunted dwarfism
High daytime reflective glare heating soil uncomfortably then cooling sharply

remediation_steps.action: Mountain Bog Peat and Sedge Mud Binding
remediation_steps.materials: Fibrous dark peat dug from alpine wetland hollows
remediation_steps.amount: Two heaping bucketfuls worked into each pace of planting trench
remediation_steps.purpose: Acts as an enduring cellular sponge that holds twenty times its weight in water.

remediation_steps.materials: Dull flour-like silt scooped from dried stream eddy pools
remediation_steps.amount: One bucketful blended into the top hand's depth of bed
remediation_steps.purpose: Supplies the fine mineral particles missing from coarse decomposed granite.

remediation_steps.materials: Crushed campfire charcoal and partly charred pine twigs
remediation_steps.amount: A layer one finger knuckle deep laid across the top
remediation_steps.purpose: Darkens the pale sand to absorb spring solar warmth while anchoring grains against wind lift.

remediation_steps.materials: Stoneware jug of steeped rabbit pellets, nettle greens, and mountain water
remediation_steps.amount: Half a bucketful sprinkled per pace twice a moon
remediation_steps.purpose: Seeds the barren sand with living microorganisms to unlock locked stone nutrients.

soil_archetypes.name: Acidic Pine Duff Terrace
soil_archetypes.description: A thick, spongy, reddish-brown carpet of decomposing pine, fir, and spruce needles overlying rocky terrace soil. It has a springy mattress feel under boot, smells strongly of turpentine and sour tannins, and repels cold water droplets when dry.

hand_tests.procedure: Flick droplets of cold stream water from your fingertips onto dry surface duff.
hand_tests.interpretation: If droplets ball up like shiny silver beads and skate across the needles without soaking in for the count of twenty breaths, the duff is waxy and water-repellent.

hand_tests.procedure: Mix two fingertips of wood ash into a palmful of wet duff paste and listen closely next to your ear.
hand_tests.interpretation: A faint prickling hiss or rapid softening of the acrid smell confirms high acidity that will lock out brassicas and beans unless neutralized.

hand_tests.procedure: Step down firmly with your heel and lift your boot.
hand_tests.interpretation: If the earth springs back up immediately like wool fleece, seed-to-soil contact will fail; seeds will dangle in air pockets and dehydrate.

hand_tests.procedure: Examine the sub-surface duff under daylight.
hand_tests.interpretation: Bright reddish-orange needles indicate fresh, sour, nitrogen-robbing decay; dark chocolate-brown crumbly dust indicates well-rotted usable humus.

hand_tests.procedure: Flip over a flat slate resting on the duff bed and inspect the undersurface.
hand_tests.interpretation: Thick white spiderweb fungal threads show active decomposition, but an absence of worms indicates the acidity is still too sour for garden crops.

dominant_failures: Excessive acidity stunting root tips and locking out vital nutrients
Hydrophobic waxy surface shedding life-giving spring showers
Nitrogen theft by unrotted woody resinous needles
Fluffy airy structure leaving young roots unsupported

remediation_steps.action: Deep Raking of Coarse Surface Needles
remediation_steps.materials: Stiff branch rake or clawed stick
remediation_steps.amount: Remove the top two finger-depths of fresh red needles to the compost cairn
remediation_steps.purpose: Stops fresh resinous oils and sour tannins from continuing to leach into the seedbed.

remediation_steps.materials: Sifted wood ash from the hearth fire, rich in lime and potash
remediation_steps.amount: Three generous handfuls dusted across every pace of bed
remediation_steps.purpose: Neutralizes the sour pine vinegar acids and unlocks minerals for hungry cold-weather roots.

remediation_steps.materials: Campfire-calcined animal bones and wild bird eggshells hammered to coarse meal on flat rock
remediation_steps.amount: Two handfuls worked into each planting hole
remediation_steps.purpose: Provides long-lasting sweetening calcium to balance acidic soil water permanently.

remediation_steps.action: Firming Heel-Tread and Wet Loam Blending
remediation_steps.materials: Heavy subsoil loam from ditch digging and foot tamping
remediation_steps.amount: Two bucketfuls of dense earth per pace, tamped firm with boots
remediation_steps.purpose: Collapses excessive air pockets and establishes dense capillary contact for seed roots.

soil_archetypes.name: Eroded Bedrock Shallows
soil_archetypes.description: Extremely shallow dirt pockets sitting directly on solid flat terrace bedrock shelf, measuring barely two to three fingers deep. Soil is a rich mixture of windblown dust and ancient moss crust, but suffers from severe lack of volume and root run.

hand_tests.procedure: Drive your index finger knuckle into the dirt until your knuckle strikes solid stone.
hand_tests.interpretation: If your second knuckle hits unyielding bedrock, root space is critically constrained; taproots like turnips and parsnips will distort into dwarfed pancakes unless mounded.

hand_tests.procedure: Scrape back dirt with a curved slate edge to reveal bedrock seam lines.
hand_tests.interpretation: Finding finger-wide cracks allows deep-rooting plants to anchor into the mountain; solid seamless slab requires raised cribbing.

hand_tests.procedure: Rest the back of your bare hand directly against the bedrock floor beneath the shallow earth at solar noon.
hand_tests.interpretation: Warm stone indicates a valuable solar heat sponge; cold stone indicates underlying permafrost or deep mountain frost that will chill roots from below.

hand_tests.procedure: Pour a drinking cup of water onto the shallow dirt layer on a slight slope.
hand_tests.interpretation: If the soil sheet glides over the slick bedrock like butter on a hot skillet, the soil will wash off the terrace edge in the first heavy mountain deluge.

hand_tests.procedure: Inspect the fringe of the soil pocket two hours after sunrise.
hand_tests.interpretation: A shrinking damp dark circle confirms moisture is evaporating from both top wind and bottom rock heat rapidly.

dominant_failures: Catastrophic root restriction causing dwarfed, deformed harvests
Terrace sheet-erosion where whole soil blankets slide off smooth bedrock
Extreme midday heat cooking shallow roots followed by freezing night chill from below
Total inability to store reserve moisture during dry spells

remediation_steps.materials: Flat mountain stones stacked without mortar along bed margins
remediation_steps.amount: Build walls two hand-spans high around the bedrock perimeter
remediation_steps.purpose: Creates a boxed container that holds soil in place and prevents sheet erosion down the mountain.

remediation_steps.action: Inverted Turfs and Rotting Log Base (Hugelkultur Step)
remediation_steps.materials: Rotten spongy birch/pine branch punk and upside-down grassy pasture turf
remediation_steps.amount: Layer one hand-span thick directly against the bedrock floor
remediation_steps.purpose: Creates a deep moisture reservoir and thermal cushion separating roots from cold bedrock.

remediation_steps.materials: Rich silt scooped from stream pools blended with dark terrace loam
remediation_steps.amount: Six bucketfuls added per pace to double the natural soil depth
remediation_steps.purpose: Provides adequate vertical depth for hardy tubers and winter greens.

remediation_steps.action: Deep Heather and Straw Surface Mulch
remediation_steps.materials: Coarse dried mountain heather twigs and wild meadow straw
remediation_steps.amount: A protective blanket three finger knuckles thick
remediation_steps.purpose: Shields shallow roots from midday solar baking and preserves fragile moisture reserves.

soil_archetypes.name: Peaty Boggy Alpine Hollow
soil_archetypes.description: Saturated, spongy, coal-black organic soil resting against the cold rear retaining wall of the terrace where seepage and snowmelt gather. Heavy with fibrous moss, cool and squelchy, smelling of swamp iron, and oozing cold water underfoot.

hand_tests.procedure: Scoop a double handful of dark soil and compress with all your upper body strength over a bucket.
hand_tests.interpretation: If cold water streams between your fingers in steady rivulets filling half a cup, the soil is dangerously waterlogged and will rot seeds within two nights.

hand_tests.procedure: Push a sharpened hazel rod into the hollow using only palm pressure.
hand_tests.interpretation: If the rod slides effortlessly past your elbow before meeting resistance, you have a deep peat reservoir rich in organic carbon that only needs drainage and warming.

hand_tests.procedure: Examine the water standing in fresh boot prints under angled sunlight.
hand_tests.interpretation: An oily, iridescent biological film with rusty orange sediment reveals stagnant iron-rich groundwater that must be flushed with moving ditches.

hand_tests.procedure: Mold a ball of damp peat, drop it onto a flat stone from knee height.
hand_tests.interpretation: If it bounces or deforms into a rubbery puck without crumbling, the organic matter is unrotted and needs aeration and hearth ash to awaken biological decay.

hand_tests.procedure: Dig a hand-depth slice at early morning and inspect the soil profile.
hand_tests.interpretation: Hidden vertical needles of underground ice indicate deep ground frost that will remain locked in wet peat long into the growing season unless drained.

dominant_failures: Chronic oxygen starvation and root rot from standing snowmelt seepage
Deep cold retention acting as an underground refrigerator that stalls germination
Sour organic acidity locking up soil phosphorus
Severe frost heaving throwing young plants out of the ground

remediation_steps.materials: Fist-sized scree rocks and flat capping slates
remediation_steps.amount: One drainage trench one forearm deep cut along the rear wall to an outlet
remediation_steps.purpose: Draws standing mountain seepage away from beds and drops the subterranean water level.

remediation_steps.materials: Peat excavated from flanking ditches flipped on top of central beds
remediation_steps.amount: Mound beds knee-high above the surrounding terrace floor
remediation_steps.purpose: Lifts the root zone into warmer ambient air and provides free gravitational drainage.

remediation_steps.action: Heavy Mineral Hearth Ash and Crushed Slate Dressing
remediation_steps.materials: Dry grey hearth ash and finely crushed mountain slate meal
remediation_steps.amount: Four generous handfuls worked into each pace of raised ridge
remediation_steps.purpose: Sweetens sour peat acids and adds heavy mineral grit to stabilize the light spongy organic mass.

remediation_steps.materials: Wooden digging paddle or trench shovel
remediation_steps.amount: Turn over big peat clods to face midday sun across the whole terrace
remediation_steps.purpose: Lets sun and mountain wind dry excess moisture and warm the cold core before seeding.

terrain_conditions.assessment_method: Visually inspect the face wall from the terrace below: the stones should lean back slightly into the mountain slope (a healthy inward batter). Place your shoulder against the upper capstones and shove firmly with full body weight; the wall should remain rigid without rocking, rattling, or shifting. Check the toe of the wall for loose bulging stones or squelching wet mud.
risks: Capstones loosening during severe freeze-thaw cycles
Hydrostatic water pressure building behind the wall after torrential mountain cloudbursts
Voles and small rodents burrowing through gravel backfill and nesting behind stones

fixes.method: Probe the lowest stone gaps with a long, flexible willow wand to dislodge collected silt, fallen leaves, and moss.
fixes.materials: Stiff willow or hazel probe, fingers
fixes.everyday_amount: Clear one weep gap every two paces along the wall base

fixes.method: Drive thin triangular slivers of hard slate into loose joints with a smooth river cobblestone mallet.
fixes.materials: Tapered slate shims, heavy cobblestone
fixes.everyday_amount: Two to three slate wedges driven per rattling capstone

fixes.method: Tamp down a ridge of dense clay loam directly behind the wall lip to direct surface runoff away from the immediate face.
fixes.materials: Firm clay soil, boot heels
fixes.everyday_amount: A raised lip one palm wide along the entire wall rim

terrain_conditions.assessment_method: Crouch at one corner of the terrace and sight your eye along the front stone edge: a pregnant belly outward indicates internal collapse. Press your palm against the protruding bulge and listen for grinding grit sounds. Check if gaps between stones are wide enough to swallow your entire hand.
risks: Catastrophic sudden blowout during heavy rain, losing the entire vegetable bed down the cliff
Massive loss of terrace topsoil and root structures in a single mud-stone slide
Severe physical injury if the terrace floor collapses beneath the gardener's footing

fixes.method: Dig an exploratory trench behind the bulging face to relieve soil weight pressing against weakened stones.
fixes.materials: Sharpened wooden digging stick, bucket
fixes.everyday_amount: A trench one hand-depth wide and two hand-spans deep cut one pace back from the wall

fixes.method: Dismantle the bulging stone pocket down to firm foundation rock, then rebuild with stones angled inward toward the hillside at a slope matching the slant of your forearm.
fixes.materials: Existing terrace stones, angular backup rubble, gravel
fixes.everyday_amount: Rebuild one arm's length span at a time until the bulge is flattened

fixes.method: Pack clean angular mountain gravel directly behind the rebuilt stones instead of rich wet soil.
fixes.materials: Coarse scree gravel free of mud
fixes.everyday_amount: Three bucketfuls of gravel packed behind each rebuilt stone course

terrain_conditions.assessment_method: Walk the outer edge where the terrace drops off to the slope below: observe crumbling soil dribbles, exposed roots of wild grass, and undercut turf ledges. Stomp your boot heel along the edge; if the lip shears off and slides downward, the edge is actively collapsing.
risks: Continuous loss of bed width, shrinking planting space moon by moon
Dry winds striking exposed plant root crowns from the cliff edge
Cold wind tunnels swirling up the slope face and freezing outer crop rows

fixes.method: Drive stout fire-hardened hardwood stakes deep into the lip edge and weave long green willow wands tightly between them.
fixes.materials: Thumb-thick hardwood stakes, flexible willow or hazel withes
fixes.everyday_amount: One stake every two paces, woven four finger-breadths high with withes

fixes.method: Stack heavy, flat mountain boulders in a stepped stair pattern along the slope base beneath the crumbling rim.
fixes.materials: Heavy two-hand mountain stones
fixes.everyday_amount: A double course of stones along the vulnerable edge

fixes.method: Cut thick mountain turf squares from outside the beds and peg them to the eroding lip with sharpened wooden pegs.
fixes.materials: Dense alpine sod, split hazel pegs
fixes.everyday_amount: Two peg-anchored sods per pace along the rim

terrain_conditions.assessment_method: Place a smooth round river pebble on bare moist ground midway across the terrace and watch if it rolls downhill. Pour a half-bucket of water and observe the flow: if it cuts tiny braided channels in the topsoil toward the front wall, the bed is not level and topsoil will slowly wash forward.
risks: Washing of light humus and seeds toward the front lip during rain
Dry upper zone near the back cliff while the front edge becomes waterlogged
Uneven seedling emergence and erratic crop growth across the width of the terrace

fixes.method: Hoe the soil into lateral ridges running strictly across the slope perpendicular to the pebble's rolling path.
fixes.materials: Hand hoe or flat digging slate
fixes.everyday_amount: One ridge one hand's depth tall every two paces

fixes.method: Scoop soil that has accumulated against the front retaining wall and transport it to the dry rear base.
fixes.materials: Carrying basket or sturdy bucket
fixes.everyday_amount: Four bucketfuls carried backward per pace of terrace

fixes.method: Stake fallen conifer poles horizontally across the bed to create mini-terraces inside the main terrace.
fixes.materials: Arm-thick rotting pine or birch poles, wooden retaining stakes
fixes.everyday_amount: One pole pinned every three paces down the terrace bed

terrain_conditions.assessment_method: Stand on the terrace at twilight on a clear calm evening. If your breath fogs heavily at your waist here while staying invisible on the upper terraces, or if you feel a palpable chilling draught pooling around your shins like stepping into cold stream water, this terrace is a sunken frost pocket.
risks: Killing frosts striking two to three weeks earlier in autumn and lingering later in spring
Freezing stagnant air settling over foliage while upper terraces escape untouched
High humidity combined with sub-freezing air causing thick killing rime frost

fixes.method: Remove the top two courses of drystone wall at the lowest corner of the terrace to create an open exit gap where cold air can pour out like draining water.
fixes.materials: Hands, pry stick
fixes.everyday_amount: A breach two paces wide lowered by two hand-spans in the outer lip

fixes.method: Build an angled dense brushwood hedge at the uphill terrace entrance to divert downward-draining mountain air around the bed rather than into it.
fixes.materials: Dense spruce branches, interlocking juniper boughs
fixes.everyday_amount: A barrier shoulder-high angled at forty-five paces toward the side gully

fixes.method: Stack dark, flat slate slabs into a knee-high pyramid in the center of the sunken bed to store midday solar heat and warm twilight air.
fixes.materials: Dark heat-absorbing slate boulders
fixes.everyday_amount: One cairn built with as many stones as you can carry in ten trips

terrain_conditions.assessment_method: Tie a light strip of cloth or dry grass blade to a chest-high stake. If it snaps violently and stays horizontal even when lower terraces seem calm, or if soil on the windward side shows scoured stone ripples with all fine leaf litter blown away, this bench is heavily wind-scoured.
risks: Wind chill dropping plant tissue warmth far below ambient air temperatures
Severe physical stem snapping and leaf shredding during mountain gales
Extreme moisture evaporation desiccating seedlings even when soil feels damp below

fixes.method: Transplant stunted, tough mountain juniper and dwarf willow along the windward terrace edge and weave them with dead brush.
fixes.materials: Wild dwarf conifer brush, hazel stakes
fixes.everyday_amount: A dense hedge waist-high along the entire windward rim

fixes.method: Excavate planting furrows one hand-depth deep below grade, throwing the excavated soil into a protective windward ridge.
fixes.materials: Digging paddle, hands
fixes.everyday_amount: Trench one hand's depth deep with a knee-high windward berm

fixes.method: Set tall, broad slate slabs vertically on edge on the windward side of each individual seedling mound.
fixes.materials: Flat slate shingles the size of a dinner plate
fixes.everyday_amount: One shield stone propped behind each crop cluster

terrain_conditions.assessment_method: Inspect the point where the terrace soil meets the vertical bedrock mountain face. Look for green liverworts, spongy bog moss, and wet stone weeping dark trickles even after several rain-free days. Push your finger into the soil near the rock; if water squirts out around your fingernail, the bench is seepage-logged.
risks: Roots rotting in freezing, stagnant groundwater against the rock face
Bed turning into a solid sheet of ground ice when the first hard autumn freeze strikes
Anaerobic souring making the inner half of the terrace toxic to vegetable crops

fixes.method: Chisel and dig a narrow stone-lined trench right along the joint between soil and rock cliff to intercept weeping water before it enters the bed.
fixes.materials: Pointed stone chisel, hammer stone, flat gutter slates
fixes.everyday_amount: A gutter one hand-span wide running the full length of the cliff joint

fixes.action: Underground Gravel Flume to Terrace Outlet
fixes.method: Channel intercepted water through a buried stone-lined channel across the terrace to spill safely over the outer wall.
fixes.materials: Flat capping slates, clean river cobbles
fixes.everyday_amount: One cross-flume packed with two bucketfuls of cobbles per pace

fixes.method: Erect a raised log retaining barrier one pace out from the weeping cliff and plant crops exclusively in the elevated soil bed.
fixes.materials: Split pine logs, stout stakes, dry terrace loam
fixes.everyday_amount: A raised bed knee-high filled with four bucketfuls of soil per pace

frost_protection.materials_needed: Dark, heavy mountain slate slabs, dark river cobblestones, dry moss for chinking
procedure: 1. Collect dark, dense river cobbles or slate fragments the size of your two fists from sunny stream banks.
2. Arrange three to four stones in a tight ring encircling each plant's stem, resting them two fingers away from the tender stalk.
3. Tilt the stones so their widest, flattest face angles upward toward the noon sun to maximize daytime heat absorption.
4. Chink the tiny gaps between stones with dry fluffy moss to trap warm air pockets next to the stem.
5. Leave stones in place throughout the season; they store daytime heat and radiate warmth directly into the root collar all night long.
frost_protection.temperature_benefit: Prevents stem-freezing crust from forming at ground level and maintains warmth around the root collar comparable to the warmth of a sun-soaked afternoon rock well past the midnight hour.
frost_protection.when_to_apply: At initial planting time or whenever clear, windless starry nights threaten early or late frosts.
frost_protection.when_to_remove: Permanent installation throughout the mountain season; adjust stones outward as plant stems expand.
warnings: Do not allow heavy stones to lean directly against tender herbaceous stems, as abrasive winds can chafe and sever the stalk.
Ensure stones are dark-colored; pale white quartz reflects heat away instead of absorbing it.

frost_protection.materials_needed: Dense, fresh green boughs of spruce, fir, or pine gathered from lower mountain gullies
procedure: 1. Cut branch fans as long as your forearm from healthy conifer trees using a sharp hand blade.
2. Lay the boughs across the vegetable beds like overlapping roof shingles, with cut stem ends pointing into the wind.
3. Ensure the needles arch convexly over the seedlings, creating a protected tent of still dead air one hand-span above leaves.
4. Weight down the edges of outer boughs with heavy stones so mountain gales do not fling the blanket off the terrace.
5. Double the thickness over tender crops when the sky turns crystal clear and evening stars sparkle with brittle brightness.
frost_protection.temperature_benefit: Buffers against biting sub-freezing winds and stops crystal hoarfrost needles from settling on soft leaf surfaces, saving foliage from black frost bite.
frost_protection.when_to_apply: Apply two hours before sundown when evening air turns crisp and your breath begins to show distinctly.
frost_protection.when_to_remove: Lift gently in mid-morning once the sun has struck the terrace and the frost on the needles has fully melted into water droplets.
warnings: Never leave heavy needle blankets on during sunny days; trapped heat and blocked light will cause seedlings to grow pale, weak, and leggy.
Do not drop boughs directly onto brittle, frozen plants; place them gently to avoid snapping frozen leaf stems.

frost_protection.materials_needed: Tall dried mountain rye grass, sedge straw, flexible willow twigs or bark cordage
procedure: 1. Harvest armfuls of long, cured mountain grasses from dry cliff benches during late summer.
2. Tie the grass into neat sheaves as thick as your thigh using twisted bark cord or willow withes.
3. Stand three sheaves together over an individual tall plant (like kale or broad bean) in a cone-shaped mini-teepee.
4. Spread the skirt of the grass sheaves out along the ground and pin it with fist-sized rocks to stop draft infiltration.
5. Leave a two-finger vent hole at the very apex to let excess daytime moisture escape while retaining warmth.
frost_protection.temperature_benefit: Provides thick, hollow-stem dead-air insulation that shields delicate plants from severe hard crust frosts and freezing sleet.
frost_protection.when_to_apply: In autumn when frost coats the grass every morning, or in early spring over newly emerged shoots.
frost_protection.when_to_remove: Open the south-facing side of the teepee during warm sunny midday hours; close and re-pin at sunset.
warnings: If grass becomes soaking wet and freezes into a solid icy sheet, its insulation is ruined; replace with dry sheaves immediately.
Watch for mice and mountain voles making winter nests inside the warm grass cones and chewing plant crowns.

frost_protection.method_name: Earth Trench Sunken Cloche with Flat Slate
frost_protection.materials_needed: Thin, broad mountain slate slabs, wooden spacer twigs, dry earth
procedure: 1. Dig planting trenches one hand's depth below the terrace surface and plant seeds or seedlings along the trench floor.
2. Rest flat slate slabs across the top of the trench at twilight, bridging from edge to edge like a stone roof.
3. Prop one end of each slate slab up with a finger-thick twig to allow gentle air exchange and avoid suffocating plants.
4. Pack loose soil along the windward side of the stones to seal against piercing mountain wind drafts.
5. Remove or slide back the slates the next morning once the ridge shadow recedes and direct sun hits the trench.
frost_protection.temperature_benefit: Traps heat radiated upward from deep terrace soil and stone walls, raising microclimate warmth enough to stop morning frostbite on tender leaves.
frost_protection.when_to_apply: Every evening during the early unpredictable spring planting window and late autumn harvest push.
frost_protection.when_to_remove: Slide open when the morning sun warms your bare face; close again two hours before the ridge shadow falls.
warnings: Slates become searing hot if left covering trenches under unbroken midday sun, effectively baking and stewing seedlings.
Ensure slate slabs are thick enough not to shatter under the weight of sudden night mountain hail or early snowfall.

frost_protection.materials_needed: Woven willow or hazel dome baskets, dried moss, shredded bark liner
procedure: 1. Weave flexible willow wands into hemispherical dome baskets the size of an upturned cooking kettle.
2. Interweave a two-finger layer of dry hanging tree moss (old man's beard) or dry sedge between the wicker ribs.
3. Invert the bell basket over individual tender plants before nightfall.
4. Press the rim two fingers deep into loose earth and place a heavy cobble stone on top of the dome to secure against wind.
5. Stack baskets in dry shelter during warm sunny weather to keep the moss lining crisp and dry.
frost_protection.temperature_benefit: Provides durable, wind-impermeable protection that wards off sudden mountain flurries and moderate crusting frosts.
frost_protection.when_to_apply: Place over young transplants on any evening when cloudless skies and dropping twilight indicate a freeze.
frost_protection.when_to_remove: Lift off as soon as morning frost has vanished from the surrounding weeds.
warnings: Do not allow moss filling to become saturated with rain; wet moss freezes into an icy dome that chills the plant inside.
Make sure the basket is wide enough that leaves do not press against the outer woven wall where frost conducts directly.

frost_protection.materials_needed: Dry kindling, damp peat, rotten punk wood, green conifer needles, old damp moss
procedure: 1. Build a small dry wood base fire on a flat slate at the windward corner of the terrace where cold night drafts enter.
2. Once small bright coals form, smother the flames with two armfuls of damp rotten punk wood and wet moss.
3. Top the pile with fresh green spruce boughs to produce a thick, heavy, low-crawling white smoke blanket.
4. Ensure the smoke drifts gently across the surface of the beds, hanging like a dense river fog over the vegetation.
5. Tend the smoldering mound through the coldest hours between the third watch of night and daybreak.
frost_protection.temperature_benefit: Creates an artificial cloud blanket that stops radiant heat from escaping into the open mountain night sky, preventing leaf temperature from dipping to the freeze point.
frost_protection.when_to_apply: During calm, dead-still, bone-chilling inversion nights when frost is imminent and winds are light.
frost_protection.when_to_remove: Allow the smoke heap to burn out into ash once direct sunlight reaches the terrace floor.
warnings: Never use roaring open flames near dry mulch or wooden terrace stakes; keep fire contained to damp smoldering coals.
Do not use on nights with raging mountain winds; strong gusts will disperse smoke instantly and waste fuel.

frost_protection.materials_needed: Sun-warmed water from terrace warming basins, deep straw or dried grass mulch, watering bucket
procedure: 1. Ensure deep straw or leaf mulch is packed around the base of plants, keeping leaves clean and elevated.
2. Fill buckets from the shallow slate sun-basin an hour before sundown while water is still comfortably warm to the touch.
3. Gently drench the soil and lower mulch layers around root zones, being careful not to wet the leaves themselves.
4. As the sun sets, the warm damp earth and mulch slowly release latent moisture heat throughout the dark hours.
5. The releasing steam creates a localized micro-climate of gentle warmth immediately beneath the crop foliage.
frost_protection.temperature_benefit: Harnesses the high latent heat capacity of water to buffer soil temperatures, keeping ground above freezing throughout a moderate frost event.
frost_protection.when_to_apply: On evenings when sudden cold air rolls off glaciers but daytime sun was bright enough to warm basin water.
frost_protection.when_to_remove: No removal needed; allow moisture to nourish roots as normal during subsequent sunny days.
warnings: Never use icy stream water straight from snowmelt runoff; cold shock combined with freezing air will kill plants outright.
Avoid wetting crop leaves late in the day; water droplets on foliage will freeze into ice lenses that rupture plant cells.

frost_protection.materials_needed: Moundable terrace loam, flat slate shingles, wooden tamping paddle
procedure: 1. Walk along planting rows and pull loose, crumbly soil up around plant stalks using a wooden paddle or both hands.
2. Hill earth up to the lowest green leaves, burying lower stems and dormant buds beneath insulating soil.
3. Smooth the side of the dirt berm with the flat of your palm so cold wind slides over rather than cutting into the mound.
4. Shingle the windward side of the earth mound with overlapping slate fragments for armor.
5. After the cold snap passes, gently pull back half the mounded earth to let sunlight warm the main stem again.
frost_protection.temperature_benefit: Insulates vulnerable root collars and basal growth nodes within the thermal mass of the mountain earth, surviving hard freezes that burn top foliage.
frost_protection.when_to_apply: In late autumn as crops reach final maturity, or before a forecast multi-day freezing storm.
frost_protection.when_to_remove: In spring, pull back once danger of hard frost passes; for root crops, leave mounded until harvest.
warnings: Do not smother the central growing heart of leafy brassicas; keep the very center bud open to the air.
Ensure earth used for hilling is friable and dry; heavy soaking wet mud will freeze into an unyielding block of ice around stems.

crops.name: Mountain Fingerling Potato
crops.soil_needs: Loose, stone-sieved sandy loam enriched with rotted leaf duff and hearth ash; dislikes heavy sticky clay.
crops.planting_depth: One hand's depth deep into trench bottom
crops.spacing: One boot length between seed tubers, two paces between trench rows

growth_stages.duration_description: About two hand-counts of days (10 to 14 days) after planting in warming earth
growth_stages.care_notes: Watch for purple and green tips breaking soil; hill earth over them as soon as they reach two finger heights.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Tender new sprouts will blacken under light frost; keep completely buried under soil until hard freezes pass.

growth_stages.duration_description: Three to four weeks of vigorous sun growth
growth_stages.care_notes: Hill up soil twice more, creating broad ridges knee-high; dress with two handfuls of wood ash per pace.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Top foliage tolerates light frost with minor leaf margin bronzing; cover with conifer boughs if frost threatens hard crust.

growth_stages.duration_description: Three to four weeks while white or violet blossoms show
growth_stages.care_notes: Provide steady sun-warmed water; never let soil dry out completely or tubers will become knobby and cracked.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Foliage handles moderate frosts; stones tucked around base protect subterranean tuber swelling.

growth_stages.duration_description: Two to three weeks as leaves wither and die back
growth_stages.care_notes: Cease all watering to let potato skins cure and toughen inside the dry earth.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Hard frost kills dead haulms completely, which actually improves storage skin toughness; tubers remain safe underground.

ripeness_signs: Vines turn completely yellow, collapse flat against the soil, and wither to dry brown cords
Test tuber dug from the ridge edge has a firm skin that does not rub off under heavy thumb pressure
Tubers separate cleanly from stolon roots without tearing wet flesh
crops.harvest_method: Plunge a smooth wooden digging paddle two finger-widths outside the ridge center, lift gently, and sift tubers from the crumbly soil with your fingers without piercing skin.
crops.storage_notes: Dry unwashed tubers on flat slate in the shade for one afternoon until surface dirt is powdery. Store in dark dry bins cushioned with dried bracken fern. Keep completely dark to prevent poisonous greening.
crops.season_fit_logic: Must be planted as soon as soil thaws to hand's depth. Because tubers cure underground, the crop can withstand an early autumn freeze that destroys the top vines without losing the caloric harvest.

crops.name: Purple Top Winter Turnip
crops.soil_needs: Thin stony loam or sandy scree with moderate leaf mould; tolerates low fertility and cool soil.
crops.spacing: One hand span apart along rows, one boot length between rows

growth_stages.duration_description: Five to seven days after planting
growth_stages.care_notes: Thin seedlings aggressively to one palm-width apart; crowded turnips produce only wiry strings.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Tiny seedlings easily survive light ground frost with zero leaf scorch.

growth_stages.duration_description: Two to three weeks of rapid leafy expansion
growth_stages.care_notes: Harvest outer tender greens for survival salads, leaving the central heart intact.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Foliage darkens and thrives in cold; light frosts trigger sugar accumulation.

growth_stages.duration_description: Two to three weeks while root shoulders push above soil
growth_stages.care_notes: Dust wood ash around roots to deter root maggot flies; water with lukewarm stream water once a week.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Shoulders exposed to freezing air should be hilled with loose soil or straw mulch.

ripeness_signs: Purple-capped root shoulder pushes clearly above ground, measuring as wide as a clenched fist
Root feels rock-solid and heavy when gripped and squeezed between thumb and fingers
Lower foliage begins to develop a dull purple-bronze hue
crops.harvest_method: Grip the base of the leaf stems firmly at ground level and pull straight upward with a slight twisting motion. Sever the greens two finger-widths above the crown with a sharp blade.
crops.storage_notes: Store firm roots in wooden boxes packed in dry sand or dry mountain sawdust in a frost-free shelter cellar. Do not wash roots before storing.
crops.season_fit_logic: One of the fastest survival roots available. Can be sown mid-season after early greens are eaten, or sown late for an autumn harvest because frost actually improves root sweetness.

crops.name: Siberian Curled Kale
crops.soil_needs: Stony clay loam enriched with aged sheep or bird manure and wood ash; needs firm soil anchorage.
crops.spacing: Two hand spans apart in all directions

growth_stages.duration_description: Seven to ten days after sowing
growth_stages.care_notes: Firm soil around tiny stems with thumbs so mountain winds do not spin and break them.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Unbothered by freezing mornings; cells flex without bursting.

growth_stages.duration_description: Four weeks of steady vigorous branching
growth_stages.care_notes: Begin harvesting lowest mature leaves when they reach the length of your hand; plant keeps growing from center.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Tolerates repeated moderate frosts without any shelter.

growth_stages.duration_description: Indefinite survival throughout late autumn and winter snow
growth_stages.care_notes: Hill soil up to the lower leaf scars; bank with spruce boughs if snow is light and freezing wind is severe.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Thrives through hard freezing crusts; starches convert to rich sugars, making leaves taste exceptionally sweet.

ripeness_signs: Leaves reach the size of your open hand and develop tightly crinkled, ruffled edges
Leaf color turns deep blue-green with a frosty waxy bloom on the surface
Texture is crisp and snaps cleanly when bent backward
crops.harvest_method: Snap off outer, lowest leaves by pressing down firmly at the base of the leaf stem. Never cut the central apical bud.
crops.storage_notes: Best left living directly in the mountain terrace bed under snow. Harvest fresh even from under snow cover. Picked leaves stay crisp for one moon if hung in cool damp root cellar.
crops.season_fit_logic: The supreme mountain survival green. Does not care if season ends abruptly; it will stand through blizzards and continue providing living vitamins long after all other crops have ceased.

crops.name: Black Spanish Winter Radish
crops.soil_needs: Deep stone-cleared sandy loam with good drainage; excess manure causes splitting.
crops.spacing: One palm width between plants, one boot length between rows

growth_stages.duration_description: Four to six days
growth_stages.care_notes: Thin seedlings promptly; keep weeded of aggressive mountain sorrel.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Impervious to early autumn light frost.

growth_stages.duration_description: Three weeks of rough, bristly leaf development
growth_stages.care_notes: Keep soil evenly moist with warmed water so roots do not become woody or hollow.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Rough leaves laugh off frost needles.

growth_stages.duration_description: Three to four weeks of tuberous expansion
growth_stages.care_notes: Hill earth over black root tops as they push out of the ground.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Root withstands hard freezes while buried under earth and snow.

ripeness_signs: Roots reach the size of a goose egg or large fist with rough, sooty-black charcoal skin
Flesh inside is brilliant solid white and dense as turnip
Pungent peppery aroma when skin is scratched with a fingernail
crops.harvest_method: Ease a wooden lever stick beneath the bulb and lever upward while pulling the bristly foliage.
crops.storage_notes: Remove leaves by twisting. Pack unwashed black roots in wooden crates filled with dry moss or sand. Keeps sound for three to four moons without shriveling.
crops.season_fit_logic: Sown after the summer solstice as days shorten. Fits into late mountain summer when warm-weather plants fail, thriving in declining autumn temperatures.

crops.name: Highland Naked Barley
crops.soil_needs: Poor, shallow stony terrace soil; requires good drainage and high midday light; tolerates cold gravel.
crops.spacing: Broadcast evenly so seeds sit two fingers apart, or sown in furrows one boot length apart

growth_stages.duration_description: Three to four weeks from sowing
growth_stages.care_notes: Tamp soil firm with boots after sowing so seeds make hard contact; weed out broadleaf competitors.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Dense young grass blades easily survive severe frosts and dusting snow.

growth_stages.duration_description: Three weeks as stalks shoot skyward to knee-height
growth_stages.care_notes: Shield from violent terrace gales with edge wattling; requires sun to strengthen straw.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Frost during jointing can cause kinked stems; keep windbreaks intact.

growth_stages.duration_description: Two to three weeks while long bristle awns wave in wind
growth_stages.care_notes: Keep birds away using fluttering cloth strips or rattling slate clappers.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Tolerates moderate frosts, but severe freeze during milky grain stage shrinks kernels.

growth_stages.duration_description: Two weeks of solar drying
growth_stages.care_notes: Stop all water; stalks turn dry golden yellow.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Fully hardened grain is completely immune to autumn frosts.

ripeness_signs: Seed heads nod heavy and crook downward toward the earth
The entire stalk and awn bristles turn brittle, shining golden amber
A grain kernel bitten between front teeth cracks with a clean sharp snap rather than squishing doughy
crops.harvest_method: Shear stalks one palm-width above ground using a curved hand sickle or sharp slate blade. Tie into tight sheaves and cure in sunny stooks for three days.
crops.storage_notes: Thresh kernels from heads by beating inside a leather sack. Sift out chaff in a stiff mountain breeze. Store clean, dry naked grains in tightly covered clay jars or dry timber bins.
crops.season_fit_logic: Naked barley threshes free of hull without milling equipment, providing direct human grain calories in very short, high-altitude alpine seasons where wheat or corn cannot mature.

crops.name: Hollow Crown Mountain Parsnip
crops.soil_needs: Deep, stone-picked pocket of rich loam; requires at least a forearm's depth of loose soil without stones.
crops.spacing: One hand span apart along rows, one pace between rows

growth_stages.duration_description: Three weeks of patient waiting in cold ground
growth_stages.care_notes: Mark rows with fast-germinating radish seeds so you do not accidentally hoe tiny parsnip threads.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Tiny seedlings survive cold spring snow flurries without damage.

growth_stages.stage_name: Deep Taproot Drilling and Foliage Expansion
growth_stages.duration_description: Six to eight weeks of steady summer growth
growth_stages.care_notes: Keep weeded; water deeply with warmed water during rare dry mountain spells.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Foliage handles all light and moderate summer frosts.

growth_stages.duration_description: Four weeks of freezing autumn conditions
growth_stages.care_notes: Allow hard frosts to hit foliage repeatedly; enzymes convert starches into rich winter sugar.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Completely impervious to hard freezes; roots can freeze solid in soil and thaw unhurt.

ripeness_signs: Feathery top foliage has been frosted down to limp, blackened yellow ribbons
Root crown at ground level is as broad as three fingers across with a distinct sunken hollow center
Sample root tastes distinctly sweet like wild honeycomb when chewed raw
crops.harvest_method: Never pull by the tops, which will snap off. Dig a deep trench alongside the row with a digging paddle and gently lever the long taproots sideways out of the trench wall.
crops.storage_notes: Best stored directly in the ground where they grew, protected by a knee-high layer of dry mountain straw or bracken. Dig them as needed throughout winter whenever ground can be broken.
crops.season_fit_logic: Although long in days, parsnips can remain in the frozen ground until spring thaw, effectively extending the survival harvest through the entire dead winter period.

crops.name: Broad Windsor Fava Bean
crops.soil_needs: Sturdy stony loam with clay binder and wood ash; fixes its own nitrogen; dislikes scorching heat.
crops.spacing: One boot length between plants, one pace between rows

growth_stages.duration_description: Ten to fourteen days in cold ground
growth_stages.care_notes: Thick square stems push effortlessly through gravelly soil crusts.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Seedlings easily survive ground freezes that would kill common garden beans.

growth_stages.stage_name: Square Stem Branching and Black-and-White Bloom
growth_stages.duration_description: Four to five weeks to waist height
growth_stages.care_notes: Hill soil around stems to prevent wind toppling; pinch out the growing tips once six pod clusters form to deter black aphids.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Flowers and stems withstand moderate frosts without dropping blooms.

growth_stages.duration_description: Three to four weeks as pods swell thick and fleshy
growth_stages.care_notes: Stake rows with conifer poles tied with willow cordage against violent mountain downdrafts.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Pods withstand hard freezes; thick white downy lining inside the pod cushions seeds from frost.

ripeness_signs: Pods swell as thick as your thumb and point horizontally or nod downward from the stalk
Pod skin feels velvety and thick; seeds can be felt bulging distinctly through the pod wall
Seed scar (hilum) turns from pale green to dark brown or black inside the pod
crops.harvest_method: Snap mature pods downward from the main stem with a sharp flick of the wrist. For dry storage, let pods blacken and dry crisp on the vine.
crops.storage_notes: Shelled green beans can be boiled immediately. For dry beans, shell dried pods and store hard seeds in sealed earthenware jars. Keeps viable for three years.
crops.season_fit_logic: Can be planted into cold, thawing soil weeks before other crops. Fixes precious fertility into thin mountain soils while providing dense protein in cold climates.

crops.name: Perennial Mountain Welsh Onion
crops.soil_needs: Any terrace soil including thin gravel and scree; thrives in crevices between stone walls.
crops.spacing: Four fingers apart in dense clumps along terrace edges

growth_stages.duration_description: Seven to ten days
growth_stages.care_notes: Forms dense grass-like green quills that multiply from the base.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Completely indifferent to ice and snow.

growth_stages.duration_description: Four to six weeks of steady clump expansion
growth_stages.care_notes: Harvest individual outer stems with a knife; clump continues to divide and send up new shoots.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Survives sub-freezing blizzards uninjured.

growth_stages.duration_description: Permanent year-round survival
growth_stages.care_notes: Divide overgrown clumps every two years and plant into stone wall joints.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Roots and crowns freeze solid in rock crevices without suffering mortality.

ripeness_signs: Hollow green stems reach the thickness of your index finger
Lower white shanks extend at least two finger widths above the soil
Strong, sharp, appetizing allium aroma released upon pinching
crops.harvest_method: Slice green stems one finger knuckle above the ground to allow instant re-sprouting, or pull entire clustered stems from the side of the clump.
crops.storage_notes: Best harvested fresh daily from living clumps even in winter by sweeping snow aside. Stems can also be chopped and dried on sunny slate for survival soup seasoning.
crops.season_fit_logic: Perennial and near-indestructible. Fills the hunger gap in earliest spring before any annual seed has germinated, growing as soon as the snow melts back a finger's width.

crops.name: Yellow Mountain Rutabaga
crops.soil_needs: Firm stony loam with good moisture holding; requires wood ash for dense, sweet flesh.
crops.spacing: One boot length apart, two boot lengths between rows

growth_stages.duration_description: Ten days to establish sturdy waxy leaves
growth_stages.care_notes: Thin to one boot length spacing; water with sun-warmed water.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Seedlings withstand frost without shelter.

growth_stages.duration_description: Five weeks of vigorous waxy blue leaf growth
growth_stages.care_notes: Dust with hearth ash; weeds cannot compete once canopy closes.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Foliage remains upright through repeated moderate freezes.

growth_stages.duration_description: Four to five weeks as roots swell into dense bowling-ball globes
growth_stages.care_notes: Hill earth around bulging root shoulders before killing freezes.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Hard autumn frosts dramatically enhance rich buttery sweetness.

ripeness_signs: Roots swell larger than two clenched fists together
Shoulders develop a rich purple-bronze crest with creamy golden-yellow belly
Crown neck shows distinctive ridged leaf scars
crops.harvest_method: Lever the massive root out with a stout wooden pry bar. Slice off foliage two fingers above the crown, leaving the root tap intact.
crops.storage_notes: Store in cold dry root cellar buried in dry sand or dry sphagnum moss. Rutabagas store longer than turnips, remaining rock-solid and edible until the following summer.
crops.season_fit_logic: Essential winter staple root. Higher caloric density and better keeping qualities than turnips, making it the premier survival starch for long frozen winters.

crops.name: Hardy Winter Cereal Rye
crops.soil_needs: The poorest, rockiest, most acidic terrace scree; thrives where barley and wheat starve.
crops.spacing: Broadcast generously, roughly two fingers between seeds

growth_stages.duration_description: Three to four weeks of cold autumn growth
growth_stages.care_notes: Forms a dense green turf that locks thin soil against winter wind erosion.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Will actively grow at near-freezing temperatures where other plants go dormant.

growth_stages.duration_description: Entire duration of frozen winter beneath snow
growth_stages.care_notes: Needs no care; roots hold the terrace bed together.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Immune to hard freezing; survives being entombed in solid ice.

growth_stages.duration_description: Five to six weeks after spring thaw
growth_stages.care_notes: Shoots up taller than a person's chest; produces heavy grain heads and valuable long straw.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Spring frosts do not slow its aggressive ascent.

ripeness_signs: Straw turns silver-grey and brittle
Grain heads droop downward sharply
Hard, slender blue-grey kernels snap clean between fingernails
crops.harvest_method: Reap with sickle at knee height. Tie into bundles and cure in sunny shelters.
crops.storage_notes: Thresh kernels on a clean tarp; winnow in wind. Store grain in dry vermin-proof bins. Long tough straw is kept for thatch, mattress stuffing, and frost protection blankets.
crops.season_fit_logic: Can be sown in late autumn after all other crops are harvested to protect terrace soil through winter and yield early summer grain and valuable insulating straw.

crops.name: Mountain Orach (Mountain Spinach)
crops.soil_needs: Tolerates poor, salty, or alkaline scree; grows well in thin terrace pockets.
crops.spacing: One palm width apart, one boot length between rows

growth_stages.duration_description: Four to six days
growth_stages.care_notes: Thin seedlings early; eat thinnings as tender micro-greens.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Handles frosty dawns with zero damage.

growth_stages.duration_description: Three weeks of tender leafy production
growth_stages.care_notes: Pinch flower buds to prolong succulent leaf growth; water with sun-warmed runoff.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Foliage withstands moderate frosts without turning mushy.

ripeness_signs: Leaves expand to the size of a woman's palm, succulent and arrowhead-shaped
Color is vivid ruby-red or deep matte green with a frosted dusty undersurface
Leaves feel thick, crisp, and salty-sweet to the tongue
crops.harvest_method: Pinch individual leaves from stems, or cut the top hand-length of the stalk to encourage bushy side shoots.
crops.storage_notes: Best eaten fresh from the plant. Can be blanched briefly in boiling water and dried on flat slates in the sun for winter vegetable chips.
crops.season_fit_logic: Fastest leafy survival crop. Provides immediate fresh minerals and vitamins within five weeks of the mountain spring thaw.

crops.name: Dwarf Sugar Pod Pea
crops.soil_needs: Well-drained gravelly loam enriched with wood ash; fixes nitrogen; hates soggy waterlogged clay.
crops.spacing: Three fingers apart along rows supported by brushwood twigs

growth_stages.duration_description: Eight to ten days
growth_stages.care_notes: Stick dry birch and spruce twigs into the row for tendrils to climb immediately.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Young pea vines easily survive snow flurries and moderate frosts.

growth_stages.duration_description: Three weeks of climbing and flowering
growth_stages.care_notes: Keep soil moist with warmed water; mulch roots with dry grass.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Open flowers can be damaged by hard frost; cover with boughs on freezing nights.

growth_stages.duration_description: Two weeks of continuous picking
growth_stages.care_notes: Pick daily to force the vines to continue setting new flowers.
growth_stages.frost_handling: Pods withstand light frost, becoming sweeter after a chill.

ripeness_signs: Pods reach the length of your middle finger, flat and translucent green with tiny peas just beginning to bulge
Pod snaps crisply in two like a brittle twig when bent
Sweet juicy burst of flavor when eaten raw in the garden
crops.harvest_method: Hold the vine with one hand and snap the pod stem cleanly with the other thumb and forefinger to avoid tearing the root system.
crops.storage_notes: Eat immediately fresh, or dry mature pods on slates for rich split-pea winter survival soups.
crops.season_fit_logic: Early spring pioneer. Climbs brushwood to escape freezing ground winds and enriches the soil for subsequent hungry root crops.

water_management.materials: Flat slabs of dark black or purple slate, heavy mountain clay for caulking, fist-sized retaining stones
procedure: 1. Select the sunniest, most wind-sheltered terrace corner that receives earliest morning light.
2. Excavate a wide, shallow dish into the ground, no deeper than the length of your hand from wrist to fingertips and as wide as two long paces across.
3. Line the bottom and sloping sides with overlapping dark slate slabs, bedding them into wet clay mortar.
4. Divert icy snowmelt or stream water into the basin at daybreak until it reaches hand-depth.
5. Allow the water to sit motionless under the midday sun; the dark slate absorbs solar energy and transmits radiant heat into the shallow water layer.
6. By mid-afternoon, the water transforms from bone-numbing glacier chill to lukewarm bath warmth, ready for gentle garden irrigation.
water_management.purpose: Warms ice-cold mountain stream runoff before it touches plant roots, preventing cold-water shock which stuns plant vascular systems and halts growth for days.
warnings: Do not make the basin deeper than hand-depth; deep water will remain cold at the bottom.
Keep wild mountain animals and debris out by laying a coarse branch grill over the basin.

water_management.technique: Unfired Clay Olla Pot Subsurface Seeper
water_management.materials: Porous unglazed earthenware jugs or hollow clay vessels pinched from mountain stream clay, flat capping slate
procedure: 1. Dig holes between crop plants as deep as your forearm.
2. Bury the porous clay jugs up to their narrow necks, tamping loose gravelly loam firmly around their bellies.
3. Fill the jugs with warmed water from the sun-basin using a funnel or pinched bucket rim.
4. Cover the open mouth of each jug with a flat slate to prevent evaporation and keep out crawling insects and soil debris.
5. Water seeps steadily through the microscopic pores of the earthenware vessel directly into the surrounding subsoil at root level.
6. Refill the jugs every three to four days as water levels recede.
water_management.purpose: Delivers sun-warmed moisture straight to thirsty root zones beneath the surface without losing a single drop to desiccating mountain winds or surface evaporation.
warnings: Must be emptied and inverted before the deep winter freeze, otherwise expanding ice will crack and shatter the earthenware pots.
Never glaze the clay; glazed pots are impermeable and will not seep.

water_management.materials: Smooth flat river cobbles, timber flow-gate plug, hand hoe
procedure: 1. Carve a gentle, snake-like shallow trench running back and forth along the contour of the terrace bed.
2. Ensure the trench is only two fingers deep and one hand-span wide, maintaining an almost level gradient so water crawls at walking speed.
3. Line the serpentine channel with smooth black stones that absorb midday sunlight.
4. Release water from the primary supply ditch in a slow trickle during peak solar noon.
5. As the water meanders slowly over the hot stones, it absorbs atmospheric and stone heat while soaking into bed subsoils.
6. Block or open channel junctions with a carved wooden paddle plug to direct water to alternating terrace beds.
water_management.purpose: Distributes water evenly across the terrace while using distance and solar contact time to warm mountain water on the move.
warnings: Never run water down steep straight trenches; high-speed mountain runoff will gouge deep erosion gullies and strip topsoil.
Clear silt deposits from the channel turns after every mountain rainstorm.

water_management.technique: Snowmelt Gravel Settling and Decanting Tank
water_management.materials: Wooden plank box or drystone pit lined with clay, graded river gravel, coarse sand, sheep fleece filter
procedure: 1. Construct a two-stage stone chamber at the terrace inlet.
2. Pack the first chamber with coarse fist-sized stones topped with a layer of washed gravel and clean sheep fleece.
3. Direct turbid, grey snowmelt runoff into the first chamber to trap abrasive rock flour, silt, and sharp glacial debris.
4. Allow the clarified water to spill over a smooth slate weir into the second shallow settling basin.
5. Decant clean, sediment-free water from the surface of the second basin for delicate seedlings and drip pots.
water_management.purpose: Removes abrasive glacial silt and stone flour that would otherwise seal soil pores with an impermeable cement-like crust.
warnings: Wash out the sheep fleece and gravel filter bed once every moon to prevent clogging and foul sludge buildup.
Do not allow sediment runoff to flow directly onto seedbeds.

water_management.materials: Overlapping curved slate slabs, fist-sized porous pumice/lava stones or coarse charcoal
procedure: 1. Excavate a trench one forearm deep down the center line of the terrace planting bed.
2. Lay flat slate tiles along the trench floor, then build an arch or loose tunnel of coarse charcoal and fist-sized rocks.
3. Cover the rock tunnel with upside-down sod strips or thick bracken fern to stop topsoil from sifting down.
4. Backfill with garden loam and plant directly above and alongside the trench.
5. Introduce warm water into one end of the buried stone channel; water travels horizontally through the voids and wicks upward through capillary suction into root zones.
water_management.purpose: Creates a permanent underground water highway that keeps the soil surface completely dry (preventing crusting and weed sprouting) while keeping subsoils evenly damp.
warnings: Ensure the trench has zero downward slope; water must distribute evenly rather than pooling at the far end.
Do not puncture the protective sod layer when digging harvest roots.

water_management.materials: Heavy rounded granite and basalt river cobbles, hollow bark tube
procedure: 1. Dig a bowl-shaped depression the size of a cooking pot beside a high-value fruit bush or seedling clump.
2. Stack clean, cool rounded river cobbles into an open pyramid cairn inside the bowl.
3. As warm, moisture-laden mountain air cools rapidly during twilight, moisture condenses upon the cold dense cobbles.
4. Water droplets trickle down through the stone voids into the subterranean bowl directly at root depth.
5. The top stones shield the condensed moisture from the morning sun, preventing evaporation.
water_management.purpose: Harvests atmospheric dew and mountain fog moisture silently every night without needing an active stream or rain shower.
warnings: Keep the stones clean of dirt and fallen leaves; dust on stones absorbs dew before it can drip downward.
Only works in regions with high night humidity and sharp day-to-night temperature drops.

water_management.materials: Stout hollow elderberry branches or thick river reeds, horsehair or moss wick plug
procedure: 1. Cut thumb-thick hollow elderberry or reed stems as long as your forearm, clearing out soft internal pith with a hot wire or sharp stick.
2. Plug the bottom end loosely with a twist of clean sheep wool or horsehair to act as a slow-flow capillary restrictor.
3. Push the reed into the earth beside an individual plant until the bottom rests near deep roots, leaving three fingers of reed exposed above ground.
4. Pour sun-warmed water directly into the top of the reed tube using a small drinking horn.
5. The water slowly trickles directly into the root zone without wetting the cold, windy surface.
water_management.purpose: Eliminates surface water wastage and prevents soil crusting around tender individual crop plants like winter brassicas and squash.
warnings: Do not pack the wool plug too tight, or water will not seep; test flow in a cup before installing.
Mark the tops of reeds with white pebble caps so you do not snap them when working the terrace beds.

water_management.materials: Flat slate stepping stones, timber side logs, wooden support stakes
procedure: 1. Construct a miniature stepped water staircase connecting an upper supply pool to lower terrace beds.
2. Set three to four flat slate lips so water tumbles over each ledge in a thin, foaming sheet.
3. As water cascades from step to step, it churns with ambient mountain air, splashing over sun-warmed rock lips.
4. Dissolved mountain oxygen surges into the stream, while stagnant swamp gases and anaerobic smells evaporate away.
5. Direct the aerated, invigorated water directly into irrigation channels.
water_management.purpose: Infuses cold stagnant seepage water with life-giving oxygen and solar warmth, stimulating root respiration and waking up dormant soil microbes.
warnings: Ensure splash water does not erode the terrace retaining wall; line splash pools with durable slate slabs.
Shut off the riffle during freezing twilight hours to prevent ice damming.

pest_management.pest_name: Mountain Black Slugs and Shell Snails
signs_to_watch: Irregular ragged holes chewed through tender cabbage, turnip, and kale leaves overnight
Glistening silvery dried slime trails winding across stones, terrace walls, and damp earth
Seedlings cut down cleanly at the soil line with severed stems left lying on the dirt
conditions_that_favor: Prolonged overcast mountain drizzles and dense, clammy hill fog
Cool damp hiding crevices beneath loose terrace drystone walls and rotten mulch blankets
Overly wet soil beds situated in constant ridge shadow

bio_controls.method_name: Wood Ash and Crushed Eggshell Desiccant Perimeter
bio_controls.ingredients: Three double-handfuls of bone-dry hearth wood ash, two handfuls of campfire-calcined crushed wild bird eggshells
bio_controls.procedure: Spread a continuous band as wide as your palm and as deep as your thumb completely encircling vulnerable planting beds. The caustic alkaline ash and razor-sharp shell shards abrade and dehydrate the slug's moist belly.
bio_controls.timing: Apply in late afternoon before dusk; refresh immediately following any mountain drizzle that dampens the ash.

bio_controls.ingredients: Half a cup of boiled barley water fermented with wild mountain honey or sourdough scraps, shallow clay bowl
bio_controls.procedure: Sink shallow clay bowls into the soil so rims sit flush with the earth. Fill with fermented grain mash. Slugs are drawn by the yeast scent, crawl in, and drown.
bio_controls.timing: Set before sunset; empty drowned pests at dawn and top off with fresh sour mash every three days.

bio_controls.ingredients: Flat wide slate shingles, fresh turnip peelings
bio_controls.procedure: Lay flat slate shingles flat on damp ground throughout the garden with a turnip peel underneath. In the heat of the next morning, flip the slates; pick off congregating slugs hiding from the sun and feed to birds or drop into fire coals.
bio_controls.timing: Inspect every morning when the sun first hits the ridge.

companion_planting_deterrents: Drying aromatic mountain sage and wild mint strewn along bed edges

signs_to_watch: Hundreds of tiny, circular 'shotholes' peppering brassica and turnip leaves until they look like lace
Tiny shiny black or bronze specks that jump violently like fleas when you brush a hand over foliage
Stunted seedling growth and scorched, crisp leaf edges during sunny midday spells
conditions_that_favor: Dry, sunny, windy mountain afternoons with dusty, parched topsoil
Young spring brassicas and radishes struggling in nutrient-poor scree

bio_controls.method_name: Wood Ash and Fine Dust Foliar Coating
bio_controls.ingredients: Two handfuls of cold, finely sifted white hearth ash, one handful of powdery mountain silt
bio_controls.procedure: Dust the powder through a coarse cloth bag over moist morning leaves, coating both upper and lower leaf surfaces with a thin grey ghosting. The dry alkaline powder irritates beetles and prevents chewing.
bio_controls.timing: Dust at dawn while dew is still wet on foliage; reapply after heavy wind or rain.

bio_controls.method_name: Wild Garlic and Wormwood Bitter Leaf Brew
bio_controls.ingredients: Two crushed bulbs of wild rock garlic, three handfuls of bitter mountain wormwood foliage, one bucketful of hot water
bio_controls.procedure: Steep the crushed herbs in a covered bucket under the sun for two days until foul and bitter. Strain liquid through a cloth and drench infested brassica leaves using a brush whisk.
bio_controls.timing: Spray mid-morning when beetles begin jumping and feeding actively.

companion_planting_deterrents: Broadcasting wild coriander and aromatic fennel along terrace edges

pest_management.pest_name: Cabbage and Turnip Root Maggot Fly
