signs_to_watch: Suddenly wilting brassica plants that turn dull leaden-blue at midday even when soil is moist
Turnips and rutabagas riddled with dark, slimy, corkscrew brown tunnels beneath the skin
Small, headless white writhing grubs discovered feeding inside the taproot when pulled
conditions_that_favor: Cool, moist spring conditions when wild mountain cherry or serviceberry is in bloom
Fresh, unrotted animal manure spread carelessly on the terrace surface

bio_controls.ingredients: Squares of cured flexible birch bark or stiff conifer bark, flat slate stones
bio_controls.procedure: Cut hand-sized discs from fallen birch bark, slice a slit to the center, and slip the collar tightly around the seedling stem flat against the soil. Fly cannot lay eggs at the soil-stem junction.
bio_controls.timing: Fit immediately upon transplanting seedlings into beds.

bio_controls.method_name: Caustic Hearth Ash Stem Trench Drench
bio_controls.ingredients: Two cups of fresh wood ash, one cup of crushed charcoal dust
bio_controls.procedure: Tuck a collar of dry ash and charcoal directly against the base of each stem, forming a dry alkaline cone that desiccates newly hatched fly eggs.
bio_controls.timing: Apply when mountain flies first begin buzzing over warming beds in spring.

companion_planting_deterrents: Strong-smelling bruised pine needles banked against plant bases

signs_to_watch: Dull white talcum-powder spots spreading across upper leaf surfaces of peas and greens
Leaves yellowing prematurely, curling upward at margins, and withering into dry parchment
Musty, stale cellar odor hanging over shaded terrace corners
conditions_that_favor: Cold, clammy stagnant air trapped in deep terrace pockets with poor wind drainage
Shaded beds receiving fewer than three hand-spans of direct sunlight due to mountain ridge overhang
Crowded plant rows with heavy leaf contact

bio_controls.method_name: Sour Milk Whey and Hearth Ash Wash
bio_controls.ingredients: One cup of sour curds or milk whey strained from sheep or goat milk, two pinches of fine wood ash, half a bucketful of water
bio_controls.procedure: Whisk thoroughly and flick onto affected foliage with a pine twig brush. Lactic bacteria and natural salts eliminate fungal spores on the leaf cuticle.
bio_controls.timing: Apply at midday during sunny hours so the wash dries rapidly in direct light.

bio_controls.ingredients: Two double-handfuls of dried mountain horsetail grass (rich in natural glass silica), half a bucketful of boiling water
bio_controls.procedure: Simmer dried horsetail on campfire coals for half a candle's burn time, cool, and sprinkle onto crops to strengthen leaf cell walls against fungal penetration.
bio_controls.timing: Apply every seven days as a preventive shield during foggy weather.

companion_planting_deterrents: Thinning and spacing plants widely to allow brisk mountain breezes to dry leaves

signs_to_watch: Mature turnips, potatoes, and parsnips hollowed out from below with sharp chisel tooth marks
Spongy, collapsing run tunnels weaving just two fingers beneath the soil surface
Entire potato stems pulled down into holes like fishing lines
conditions_that_favor: Thick, undisturbed straw mulch left unmanaged through autumn
Loose, cavernous stone retaining walls offering endless predator-proof nesting burrows
Deep snow blankets providing covered runways for winter feeding

bio_controls.method_name: Crushed Bramble and Spiny Gorse Trench Packing
bio_controls.ingredients: Armfuls of dried, razor-sharp wild thorny brambles, rose briars, or spiny juniper twigs
bio_controls.procedure: Dig a trench one hand's depth deep along the base of stone walls and pack tightly with thorny brambles before covering with earth. Rodents cannot dig through the spiny barrier without tearing their feet and noses.
bio_controls.timing: Install during terrace bed preparation before planting.

bio_controls.method_name: Crushed Wild Garlic and Elderberry Leaf Burrow Flushing
bio_controls.ingredients: Bruised wild garlic leaves, pungent elder leaves, bucket of hot wash water
bio_controls.procedure: Stuff crushed pungent leaves deep into every active vole hole and pour in a bucket of hot bitter water to foul their runways.
bio_controls.timing: Repeat whenever fresh soil mounds appear on the beds.

bio_controls.method_name: Perimeter Stone Compaction and Boot Tamping
bio_controls.procedure: Walk the terrace perimeter daily, stomping down runway ridges and laying heavy boundary stones over soft spots to crush subterranean tunnels.
bio_controls.timing: Perform daily during morning garden checks.

companion_planting_deterrents: Elderberry branch stakes driven around perimeter
Strewing bitter wormwood and tansy clippings across mulch paths

signs_to_watch: Sturdy young seedlings cleanly felled overnight at the soil line, left lying like chopped timber
Fat, smooth, greyish-brown caterpillars curled tightly into a 'C' shape when dug up from shallow dirt
Damaged plants discovered in clusters along the terrace edge
conditions_that_favor: Beds choked with unmanaged wild grass sod during the previous autumn
Loose, dry cloddy soil where grubs can crawl rapidly at night without swimming in mud

bio_controls.ingredients: Finger-length sections of hollow elderberry twigs, hollow dried sunflower stalks, or thick birch bark cylinders
bio_controls.procedure: Split the hollow twig lengthwise, encircle the seedling stem, and push it one finger knuckle into the earth, leaving two fingers exposed above ground. The grub encounters hard wood armor and cannot bite through.
bio_controls.timing: Place around every seedling at the moment of planting.

bio_controls.procedure: At dusk, scrape back the top finger of soil around freshly severed seedlings with your fingers. The grub will be curled in the dirt within a hand-span of the victim; find it and crush it or drop into campfire.
bio_controls.timing: At dusk or immediately upon spotting a felled seedling in the morning.

companion_planting_deterrents: Drenching soil with bitter wormwood tea before seeding

signs_to_watch: Dense, grey or waxy black crusts of tiny motionless insects smothering tender new shoot tips and flower buds
Curled, puckered, twisted foliage coated in sticky sweet honeydew
Black sooty mold growing on foliage following honeydew deposits
conditions_that_favor: Lush, tender growth following excessive dung applications
Warm, dry, wind-sheltered terrace hollows where ladybird beetles and hoverflies have not yet emerged

bio_controls.ingredients: One cup of clear hearth ash water (made by soaking cold clean wood ash in water and skimming clear liquid), two drops of rendered animal fat soap, half a bucketful of stream water
bio_controls.procedure: Mix and flick forcefully onto aphid clusters with a branch brush. The alkaline wash breaks down their waxy bodies and suffocates them.
bio_controls.timing: Apply at mid-morning on sunny days.

bio_controls.ingredients: A pinch of fine gritty sand or coarse ash
bio_controls.procedure: Take the infested shoot tip gently in one hand, dip your other fingers in dry sand, and gently wipe the aphids off the stem. The grit crushes the soft-bodied insects without harming the tough stem.
bio_controls.timing: Inspect and rub at first sign of small clusters before they explode in numbers.

companion_planting_deterrents: Allowing wild mountain umbel flowers to bloom on terrace walls to attract predatory hoverflies

soil_regeneration.practice: Post-Harvest Slash and Crimped Straw Mulching
soil_regeneration.when_to_do: Immediately following the final autumn crop harvest before the first burying snowstorm.
soil_regeneration.materials: Harvest crop haulms (pea vines, bean stalks, turnip greens), long wild mountain grasses, flat river rocks
soil_regeneration.procedure: Chop harvested crop residues with a sharp spade into pieces the length of your finger. Spread them evenly over the bare beds. Top with a layer of cured mountain meadow grass as thick as your palm. Crimp and compress the straw by walking heel-to-toe across the bed, then weight down the edges with heavy slate slabs so mountain gales do not strip the blanket away.
soil_regeneration.benefit: Prevents fierce winter winds from blowing fine topsoil off the terrace, stops frost-heaving from shattering earth crumb structure, and feeds soil worms slowly under snow cover.

soil_regeneration.when_to_do: Built throughout late summer and autumn; turned once before the big freeze.
soil_regeneration.materials: Green weeds, wild nettles, animal bedding dung (rabbit, sheep, or goat), brown forest duff, wood ash, crushed bone
soil_regeneration.procedure: Construct a rectangular stone frame two paces wide against a sunny stone wall. Lay a bottom coarse layer of finger-thick birch twigs for air. Alternate layers: two hand-depths of green nitrogenous weeds and dung, one hand-depth of dry brown leaf duff, and a light dusting of white hearth ash and calcined bone meal. Cap the entire heap with a blanket of thick mountain sod to shed heavy rain and retain internal heat.
soil_regeneration.benefit: Concentrates scarce biological nutrients into rich, crumbly black gold that warms the terrace beds and restores organic sponge matter.

soil_regeneration.practice: Biochar Pit Firing with Dung Quenching
soil_regeneration.when_to_do: Mid-autumn on a dry, calm afternoon after gathering dry mountain deadfall.
soil_regeneration.materials: Dry fallen conifer branches, birch deadfall, shovel, bucket of liquid manure slurry, stream water
soil_regeneration.procedure: Dig a cone-shaped pit in the terrace subsoil one arm's length deep and wide. Build a criss-cross fire of dry deadfall from the bottom up. As flames roar and wood chars to glowing, smoking embers without white ash, smother the air by shoveling excavated earth over the pit mouth. Let char smolder for two hours, then quench the glowing coals by pouring three bucketfuls of rich dung-slurry over them. The porous charcoal absorbs the dung nutrients instantly.
soil_regeneration.benefit: Produces permanent terra preta charcoal granules that remain in thin terrace soils for generations, buffering water and providing microscopic shelters for beneficial fungi.

soil_regeneration.practice: Deep Winter Drystone Wall Chinking and Backfill Renovation
soil_regeneration.when_to_do: Late winter during mild sunny thaws when soil is resting.
soil_regeneration.materials: Flat slate shims, clean angular scree cobbles, heavy ironwood pry lever
soil_regeneration.procedure: Walk the entire face of the terrace retaining wall. Inspect every joint where stones have rattled loose from frost heaving. Drive sharp slate wedges into loose joints with a cobblestone mallet until the wall rings solid. Shovel away compacted silt choking the rear drainage zone behind the wall and repack with two bucketfuls of clean angular scree gravel per pace.
soil_regeneration.benefit: Guarantees the terrace will not suffer blowout when massive spring snowmelt surges off the high mountain ridges.

soil_regeneration.practice: Frost-Heave Stone Picking and Perimeter Bordering
soil_regeneration.when_to_do: Early spring immediately following the retreat of the winter snow blanket.
soil_regeneration.materials: Wooden collecting hod or sturdy bucket, bare hands
soil_regeneration.procedure: As frozen ground expands and contracts during spring thaws, subterranean rocks are 'born' and pushed up to the surface. Walk every bed with a bucket, gathering all frost-heaved stones larger than a walnut. Carry these stones to the outer terrace lip and stack them into the perimeter windbreak or border retaining cribs.
soil_regeneration.benefit: Gradually deepens the stone-free soil profile year after year, turning jagged scree beds into deep, workable root loam.

soil_regeneration.when_to_do: Early spring when overwintered rye and mountain vetch reach knee-height.
soil_regeneration.materials: Heavy timber log, foot ropes, wooden spade
soil_regeneration.procedure: Tie ropes to both ends of a heavy conifer log. Walk backward dragging and stomping the log over the green winter cover crop, snapping and bruising the succulent stems at ground level so they lay flat in a dense woven carpet. Do not dig or plow the roots; leave the tangled roots in the earth to rot into worm channels.
soil_regeneration.benefit: Creates an immediate, weed-suppressing, moisture-retaining living mulch blanket that feeds the soil without disturbing delicate terrace soil layers.

soil_regeneration.practice: Hearth Wood Ash and Bone Mineral Dusting
soil_regeneration.when_to_do: Late winter scattered directly over lingering snow crusts.
soil_regeneration.materials: Sifted wood ash from winter heating fires, campfire-roasted crushed animal bones
soil_regeneration.procedure: Store dry wood ash all winter in covered clay vessels. In late winter, walk the snow-covered terrace beds and broadcast the grey ash and pulverized bone meal evenly over the snow crust until the white surface turns dull mottled charcoal grey. As the sun strikes the dark ash, it absorbs heat, melting the snow two weeks earlier while carrying dissolved potash, lime, and phosphorus straight down into the thawing earth.
soil_regeneration.benefit: Accelerates spring ground thaw by two full weeks while balancing mountain soil acidity and replenishing depleted root minerals.

readiness_gates.procedure: Stand on the terrace below and plant your shoulder firmly against the center of the retaining wall face at chest height. Brace your boots and exert full body shoving force against the stones. Repeat every five paces along the entire wall length.
readiness_gates.pass_criteria: The wall feels completely monolithic and dead-solid; zero stones shift, rattle, groan, or tilt outward under your body weight.
readiness_gates.fail_action: Do not plant or fill beds! Dismantle the loose section immediately down to sound stone, repack backing gravel, and rebuild with an inward batter before adding topsoil.

readiness_gates.procedure: Kneel beside the bed at midday. Hold your fingers straight and rigid, and drive your open hand straight down into the earth using only the downward thrust of your arm, without wriggling or clawing.
readiness_gates.pass_criteria: Your fingers penetrate smoothly into loose, crumbly soil past your second knuckle (for shallow greens) or to the base of your palm (for root crops) without striking frozen ground or impenetrable stone shelf.
readiness_gates.fail_action: If your hand stops at one finger depth against cold hard ground, soil frost is still locked below; hill soil into raised ridges, cover with dark slate slabs to catch solar heat, and wait another seven suns.

readiness_gates.check_name: Soil Warmth Midday Bare-Hand Contact Gate
readiness_gates.procedure: At solar noon on a clear day, scrape away the top dry finger of soil. Press the tender inside wrist or bare palm flat against the damp subsoil and hold it motionless for the count of thirty slow breaths.
readiness_gates.pass_criteria: The earth feels neutral or mildly comforting like a sun-warmed stone; no deep, bone-aching ache or numbness creeps into your wrist bones.
readiness_gates.fail_action: If your palm goes numb with an icy ache within twenty breaths, the ground is an ice-box; seeds will rot in the dirt before germinating. Install slate heat batteries and wait for mountain dandelions to open.

readiness_gates.check_name: Drainage Mud Squeeze and Ribbon Gate
readiness_gates.procedure: Scoop a handful of earth from two knuckles deep. Squeeze it into a ball in your fist, then open your hand. Drop the ball from belt height onto a flat stone.
readiness_gates.pass_criteria: The ball holds together in your palm without water glistening or oozing between your fingers, and when dropped, it shatters cleanly into crumbly, friable crumbs.
readiness_gates.fail_action: If cold water squelches out between your knuckles, or if the dropped lump lands with a dull thud like sticky modeling clay, the soil is waterlogged. Cut drainage channels and delay planting to prevent seed drowning.

readiness_gates.procedure: Before dropping a single seed in the ground, walk the perimeter and count your stockpiled protective gear: conifer boughs, dry grass bundles, flat slate tiles, wicker cloches, and dry hearth ash.
readiness_gates.pass_criteria: You possess enough boughs, straw stooks, and slate shingles stacked ready beside the beds to cover every single planted row within the time it takes to walk the terrace twice.
readiness_gates.fail_action: Halt planting! A sudden mountain frost will wipe out unprotected shoots overnight. Spend the day in the conifer woods harvesting boughs and collecting slate slabs before sowing seeds.

readiness_gates.check_name: Water-Warming Basin Integrity and Supply Gate
readiness_gates.procedure: Fill your slate-lined sun-warming basin to hand's depth at sunrise. Check water level at noon and dip your hand into the water.
readiness_gates.pass_criteria: The basin holds its water without clay-seam leaks, and the midday water feels distinctly tepid and comfortable to a submerged hand, not ice-numbing.
readiness_gates.fail_action: If the basin leaks empty, recaulk seams with heavy mountain clay and pounded silt. If water remains freezing, increase slate lining or reduce water depth to four fingers.

readiness_gates.check_name: Predator Burrow and Rodent Exclusion Gate
readiness_gates.procedure: Carefully inspect the junction where the terrace soil meets the retaining wall and cliff face. Look for fresh dime-to-fist-sized holes, chewed roots, or fresh soil mounds thrown up by mountain voles and mice.
readiness_gates.pass_criteria: No open, active burrows or soft collapsed runway tunnels are detected within three paces of planting rows.
readiness_gates.fail_action: Pack all holes immediately with crushed spiny juniper twigs and pungent wild garlic mash, tamp down with cobblestones, and set deadfall traps before seeding.

readiness_gates.check_name: Windbreak Integrity and Gale Buffer Gate
readiness_gates.procedure: Stand on the windward terrace lip during an afternoon breeze. Crouch down to the height of an emerging seedling (one hand-span above bed level) and feel for wind draughts with your face.
readiness_gates.pass_criteria: The windbreak wattle or dead-hedge deflects the gale upward over your head; air at seedling level is calm enough that a dry seed fluff or dandelion seed drops gently to earth rather than blowing horizontally away.
readiness_gates.fail_action: Weave additional pine boughs and brush into the windward wattle fence until ground-level drafts are halted.

season_reasoning.scenario: Hyper-Short Mountain Season (Fewer than Two Full Moons / Under 60 Days)
season_reasoning.frost_date_assessment_method: Watch the high mountain snowline and natural indicator plants: the season opens only when wild alpine yellow dandelions bloom on exposed sunny scree and the snowline retreats higher than two arrow-shots above the terrace. The season closes when mountain swallows depart and the first dusting of snow coats the ridge behind the terrace overnight.
decision_rules: IF estimated growing window is under two full moons, THEN eliminate all long-season root crops (parsnips, rutabagas) immediately.
IF rapid calories are required, THEN plant exclusively 45-day purple top turnips, fast mountain orach greens, and quick winter radishes.
IF potatoes are planted, THEN pre-sprout seed tubers in sunny, sheltered cliff nooks for two weeks before planting to gain a ten-day head start.
IF frost threatens during flowering, THEN deploy conifer boughs and smudge fires immediately, as there is zero time for crops to recover from setbacks.
warning_signs: Glacial ice needles fail to melt from shaded ditch banks even at high noon
Mountain crickets cease chirping at twilight three days in a row
Puffballs and wild shelf mushrooms harden and burst into dry brown powder
Flocks of high-altitude finches congregate and fly down-valley toward lower foothills

season_reasoning.scenario: Standard Mountain Terrace Season (Two to Three Full Moons / 60 to 80 Days)
season_reasoning.frost_date_assessment_method: Season commences when wild mountain birch buds swell and break into tiny green mouse-ear leaves, confirming ground thaw. Season terminates when heavy white rime frost coats the grass stems three mornings in succession and does not melt until the sun is three hand-spans above the horizon.
decision_rules: IF season spans two to three moons, THEN prioritize mountain fingerling potatoes, broad fava beans, and siberian curled kale as primary caloric staples.
IF broad fava beans reach waist height with six pod clusters, THEN pinch out apical tips immediately to divert all plant sugars into fattening existing pods before frost.
IF spring was delayed by late blizzards, THEN shift planting area to early turnips and cut-and-come-again mountain greens.
IF root crops have formed globes the size of a fist by late season, THEN allow light autumn frosts to kiss the foliage to sweeten flavor before pulling.
warning_signs: Birch and wild aspen leaves turn butter-yellow along the high ridge slopes
Morning ice skins on the water warming basin require a firm thumb press to crack
Sun sinks behind the southern mountain ridge two hand-widths earlier each afternoon
Night condensation turns to brittle white crust rather than wet liquid dew

season_reasoning.scenario: Extended Sheltered Terrace Season (Three to Four Full Moons / 80 to 110 Days)
season_reasoning.frost_date_assessment_method: Occurs on south-facing lower terraces shielded by high cliff headwalls that reflect solar warmth. Season starts when wild mountain nettles shoot up one hand-span tall in cliff crevices and ends when ground freezing locks soil deeper than two finger knuckles.
decision_rules: IF terrace benefits from three to four moons of growth, THEN allocate one full bed to deep hollow crown mountain parsnips and yellow rutabagas for long-term winter survival storage.
IF space permits, THEN stagger sowings: plant fava beans and barley first, followed by turnips and greens, followed by a second succession of winter radishes.
IF cereal rye is available, THEN broadcast rye seed between mature crops thirty suns before the final freeze to establish winter erosion cover.
warning_signs: Mountain sheep descend from high alpine pastures to graze lower terrace scrub
Bracken fern across open slopes dies back to crisp rust-red skeletons
Water in clay olla pots freezes into solid plugs by the third hour after sunset
Sunlight ceases hitting the rear terrace wall as the winter sun arc flattens

season_reasoning.scenario: Sun-Deprived Ridge Shadow Season (Severely Limited Daily Direct Sunlight)
season_reasoning.frost_date_assessment_method: Track the daily travel of the high cliff shadow across the terrace beds using stone markers. The growing season in deep shadow is governed not by calendar moons but by the narrow window when direct sunlight clears the ridge peak for at least four candle-burns of time per day.
decision_rules: IF terrace receives fewer than four candle-burns of direct sunlight daily, THEN banish all fruiting crops and grains (barley, peas) to sunnier ground.
IF planting in shadow, THEN cultivate exclusively cold-tolerant leafy greens (kale, mountain orach, welsh onions) which thrive in diffuse cool light.
IF soil stays cool and sluggish in shadow, THEN mound earth into steep 45-degree ridges tilted directly toward the brief midday sun angle.
IF mildew signs appear on leaves due to shade and cold dampness, THEN spray immediately with wood ash wash and thin plants aggressively to maximize air flow.
warning_signs: Soil surface remains permanently damp and grows dark green liverwort scum
Ridge shadow creeps across the terrace before midday has even passed
Morning dew on leaves fails to evaporate throughout the entire daylight period
Stems become pale, spindly, and stretch horizontally toward the sunlit cliff edge

season_reasoning.scenario: Wind-Scoured Exposed Shoulder Season (High Wind Chill and Constant Evaporation)
season_reasoning.frost_date_assessment_method: Observe wind patterns: season opens when fierce downdraft winter blizzards give way to intermittent valley thermal breezes. Season ends abruptly when dry polar gales howl out of the north, desiccating soil and dropping effective wind chill below freezing long before official winter snowfall.
decision_rules: IF terrace is subjected to continuous gales, THEN prune plant canopies low and grow only dwarf, ground-hugging crops (turnips, radishes, dwarf peas).
IF tall crops like barley or fava beans are attempted, THEN plant in sunken trenches two finger-knuckles below the soil line behind stout wicker hurdles.
IF high winds cause rapid topsoil drought, THEN apply twice the normal volume of rotting sod and leaf mulch to anchor soil moisture.
IF cold winds threaten to freeze tender shoots during sunny days, THEN keep windward slate cloches erect even at midday to break wind velocity.
warning_signs: Topsoil scours into airborne dust ripples and blows off terrace edges
Leaf margins of hardy kale curl inward and turn brittle as dry parchment
Stout wooden stakes lean permanently down-valley from relentless wind pressure
Evening breeze smells sharp and dry like powdered stone rather than damp earth

season_reasoning.scenario: Untested First Survival Season (Unknown Duration and Uncharted Microclimate)
season_reasoning.frost_date_assessment_method: Triage strategy: assume the shortest possible mountain season (no more than 50 frost-free days). Keep daily observational tallies on a notched cedar stick, noting sunny days, frosty dawns, and cloudbursts.
decision_rules: IF terrace microclimate history is entirely unknown, THEN split beds: 50 percent fast insurance crops (turnips, radishes, greens), 30 percent hardy staples (potatoes, fava beans), and 20 percent frost-proof perennials (welsh onions).
IF unexpected hard frost strikes mid-season, THEN record which crops survive untouched to guide seed saving for subsequent years.
IF crops mature earlier than expected and season holds mild, THEN immediately sow a second catch crop of quick radishes and winter greens.
warning_signs: Wild mountain berries on slopes drop to the ground while still hard and sour
Sudden plunge in bird activity across the terrace benches
Dusk temperature drops from comfortable hand warmth to breath-fogging cold in fewer breaths than it takes to eat a bowl of broth
High clouds race rapidly from the north while ground air remains eerily dead still

season_reasoning.scenario: Early Autumn Killing Freeze Pattern (Sudden Premature Winter Incursion)
season_reasoning.frost_date_assessment_method: Watch the high mountain passes: when storm clouds pile up thick and dark like bruised iron over the northern peaks and barometric pressure drops rapidly (indicated by smoke from campfire curling down to the ground rather than rising), an early killing freeze is 24 hours away.
decision_rules: IF killing freeze is imminent, THEN conduct an emergency harvest of all mature and semi-mature potatoes, turnips, and bean pods immediately.
IF root crops like parsnips and rutabagas must remain in ground, THEN heap every available armful of straw, dry grass, and soil over their crowns.
IF immature potato haulms are frozen to black mush, THEN cut dead vines away immediately at soil level to prevent rot from traveling down into tubers.
IF greens are lightly frozen in morning, THEN do NOT touch or walk on them; allow the gentle midday sun to thaw them gradually in place.
warning_signs: Campfire smoke refuses to rise, drifting along the ground and stinging eyes
Mountain springs bubble with crystal-clear, icy water colder than ice itself
Dead calm air with sky turning milky white and brittle blue at the zenith
Night stars twinkle with extraordinary, razor-sharp intensity without twinkling haze

sunlight_assessment.procedure: On the first clear day of the season, walk the terrace at mid-morning when the towering mountain ridge shadow retreats. Place a white river pebble along the ground exactly where the shadow edge rests. Return at solar noon and place a second pebble; return two candle-burns before dusk and place a third pebble. Repeat this process every full moon. By sighting along the rows of marker pebbles, you create a permanent seasonal map of shade boundaries across your terrace.
sunlight_assessment.what_it_tells_you: Reveals precisely which terrace zones receive full direct sunlight throughout the day (ideal for potatoes, barley, and fava beans) versus zones trapped in persistent mountain shade (suitable only for cold greens, radishes, or water-warming basins).

sunlight_assessment.procedure: Stand upright at solar noon (when your shadow points directly north and is at its shortest). Stand with your back to the sun, extend your arm straight toward the horizon, and use your fist fingers stacked one above the other to measure how high the sun has climbed above the southern mountain crest.
sunlight_assessment.what_it_tells_you: Indicates the seasonal height of the sun's path. When the sun climbs more than four stacked fists above the ridge, the season is at peak solar strength; when it drops below two stacked fists, solar energy is failing and late-season crop growth will stall.

sunlight_assessment.procedure: Inspect the native boulders and bedrock cliffs flanking your terrace. Observe the color and growth of natural mosses and crustose lichens: dark green, velvety, damp moss flourishes on rock faces facing away from the sun, whereas bright golden-orange and powdery yellow crust lichens dominate rock surfaces that bake in direct southern sunlight.
sunlight_assessment.what_it_tells_you: Instantly shows the historical microclimate aspect of any terrace bench without waiting for seasonal tracking: golden rock zones are your warmest planting thermal banks, while green mossy zones are cold, shaded, and damp.

sunlight_assessment.procedure: Walk the terrace two hours after sunrise on a calm morning. Observe where the thick grey morning dew evaporates first from the soil and weeds, and where it lingers as cold moisture drops long into the midday.
sunlight_assessment.what_it_tells_you: Quickly identifies early-morning solar thermal zones. Beds that dry first receive the earliest sun, warming root zones hours ahead of lagging beds; these are your premier locations for cold-sensitive crops.

sunlight_assessment.procedure: Place broad, dark slate slabs flat on the soil in different terrace sections at sunrise. At twilight, one hour after the sun has dipped behind the mountain ridge, walk the terrace barefoot or press your bare cheek against each slate slab.
sunlight_assessment.what_it_tells_you: Identifies which terrace micro-beds act as superior thermal sponges. Slates that stay comfortably warm to the touch well into the night reveal beds with high heat capacity, ideal for planting near retaining walls to survive frost.

sunlight_assessment.procedure: In early spring as the winter snowpack begins to retreat, sketch or memorize the pattern in which the snow melts off the terrace benches. Mark the patches where bare brown earth first emerges while surrounding areas remain buried under snow.
sunlight_assessment.what_it_tells_you: Pinpoints the warmest micro-sites on the mountain terrace. These 'snowmelt islands' receive the combined benefit of maximum solar exposure, wind protection, and subterranean stone warmth, making them your earliest planting nurseries.

sunlight_assessment.procedure: In late afternoon, extend your arm fully toward the sun with your palm facing you and fingers held horizontally together. Count how many finger-widths fit between the bottom of the sun disc and the top of the towering mountain ridge.
sunlight_assessment.what_it_tells_you: Each finger width represents approximately fifteen minutes of remaining direct sunlight before the terrace is plunged into cold mountain ridge shadow. Enables precise timing for closing trench cloches, lighting smudge heaps, and spreading frost boughs before the freeze sets in.

non_instrument_sensory_compass.standard_authority: NRCS Soil Survey Field Book (Soil Depth Classes) & FAO Guidelines for Soil Description
non_instrument_sensory_compass.household_tool: Thumb-thick hazel, willow or dry pine walking stick trimmed to flat blunt tip
non_instrument_sensory_compass.body_metric: Palm width, hand-span (~20 cm), and wrist-to-elbow depth marks
non_instrument_sensory_compass.parameter: Workable Topsoil Depth & Bedrock Hardpan Detection
non_instrument_sensory_compass.zero_instrument_procedure: Carve thumb-width notches every hand-width on a dry stick. Drive the blunt tip firmly straight down into the terrace bed using steady palm-heel pressure until it hits solid impassable stone resistance. Note which notch aligns with the ground level.
non_instrument_sensory_compass.fao_nrcs_interpretation: Very Shallow (< 10 cm / under 1 hand-width): unsuitable for root crops, rosettes only. Moderately Shallow (10-25 cm / 1 hand-span): suitable for radishes, turnips, spinach. Deep (> 30 cm / forearm length): suitable for deep-rooting cold staples.
non_instrument_sensory_compass.remedial_action: If under 1 hand-span, terrace wall must be raised by 2 stone tiers and backfilled with crushed leaf mould and screened subsoil.

non_instrument_sensory_compass.standard_authority: NRCS Field Texture by Feel Chart & FAO Soil Texture Finger Assessment
non_instrument_sensory_compass.household_tool: Clear glass jar, bottle, broken window pane, or clean flat slate stone
non_instrument_sensory_compass.body_metric: Handful, finger ball, and index finger-to-thumb ribbon roll
non_instrument_sensory_compass.zero_instrument_procedure: Take a golf-ball sized handful of moist soil from knuckle depth. Knead in palm until consistency of putty. Roll between palms into a pencil-thick cylinder. Push the cylinder out over index finger with thumb, allowing it to ribbon outward until it breaks under its own weight. Separately, drop a dry clod into a clear glass jar of water and observe slaking.
non_instrument_sensory_compass.fao_nrcs_interpretation: Ribbon breaks before 2 cm: coarse sandy loam (fast drainage, low nutrient retention). Ribbon extends 2.5-5 cm: mountain loam (ideal moisture balance). Clod explodes into clouds in water: unstable aggregate prone to terrace erosion; needs humic binder.
non_instrument_sensory_compass.remedial_action: Work in 2 bucketfuls of decomposed dark leaf litter per square pace to build water-holding humus sponge.

non_instrument_sensory_compass.standard_authority: FAO Mountain Agro-Ecology & Microclimate Shadow Mapping Guidelines
non_instrument_sensory_compass.household_tool: 5 clean white chalk, quartz, or river stones placed along terrace edge
non_instrument_sensory_compass.body_metric: Paced steps, hand-width sun arc estimation (1 finger = ~15 minutes, 1 palm = ~1 hour)
non_instrument_sensory_compass.parameter: Sunlight Intensity, Ridge Occlusion & Interval Timing
non_instrument_sensory_compass.zero_instrument_procedure: Place 5 white stones in a line across the center bed: Stone 1 at morning sunbreak, Stone 2 at mid-morning, Stone 3 at solar noon (shortest shadow), Stone 4 at mid-afternoon, Stone 5 at final ridge shadow occluding the terrace. Count total hours terrace remains unshaded by mountain ridges.
non_instrument_sensory_compass.fao_nrcs_interpretation: < 4.5 unshaded hours: Severe ridge shading. Only fast-turnaround brassicas, tatsoi, radishes. Long-season tubers will starve. 6+ hours: Moderate alpine sun; sufficient for peas, turnips, cold brassicas.
non_instrument_sensory_compass.remedial_action: Paint rear terrace stone wall white or line with reflective pale slate to bounce low-angle sun rays onto bed.

non_instrument_sensory_compass.standard_authority: FAO Irrigation Water Quality for High Altitude Horticultural Production
non_instrument_sensory_compass.household_tool: Dark slate rock basin or blackened metal pot/pan
non_instrument_sensory_compass.body_metric: Inner wrist skin, thin venous plexus sensitive to cold shock (< 10 C)
non_instrument_sensory_compass.parameter: Irrigation Water Temperature & Thermal Root Shock Margin
non_instrument_sensory_compass.zero_instrument_procedure: Dip inner wrist and forearm veins into water source for 5 full breaths. If an involuntary sharp bone ache or tingling numbness occurs within 3 seconds, water is glacial melt (1-4 C). Never pour directly on crops.
non_instrument_sensory_compass.fao_nrcs_interpretation: Glacial meltwater halts root phosphorus and nitrogen uptake for 48 hours and triggers leaf chlorosis. Water must be warmed in shallow dark slate solar pans until wrist touch feels neutral, soothing, or lukewarm.
non_instrument_sensory_compass.remedial_action: Channel stream through 10-pace zigzag serpentine over dark slate or hold in wide shallow pans for 2 hours in noon sun.

non_instrument_sensory_compass.standard_authority: NRCS Soil Climate Analysis Network (SCAN) & Biological Threshold Rules
non_instrument_sensory_compass.body_metric: Dorsal skin of the hand (bare back of knuckles) pressed flat at solar noon
non_instrument_sensory_compass.parameter: Seed Germination Readiness & Root Thermal Buffer
non_instrument_sensory_compass.zero_instrument_procedure: Scrape back mulch at solar noon. Press the bare dorsal skin of hand firmly against flat mineral earth for 10 slow seconds. Feel whether heat transfers into hand, hand loses heat rapidly, or contact feels neutral.
non_instrument_sensory_compass.fao_nrcs_interpretation: Bone-cold biting chill: soil < 5 C; brassica/pea seeds will imbibe ice water and rot. Neutral to slight warmth: soil > 8-10 C; safe for immediate sowing of cold-adapted radishes, greens, and pre-chitted seeds.
non_instrument_sensory_compass.remedial_action: Cover soil with clear stone cloches, charred dark wood ash, or dry black slate tiles 3 days prior to planting to absorb solar radiation.

non_instrument_sensory_compass.standard_authority: WMO Beaufort Scale Non-Instrument Field Observation & FAO Windbreak Guidelines
non_instrument_sensory_compass.household_tool: Loose cloth strip, pine branch tip, campfire smoke drift
non_instrument_sensory_compass.body_metric: Face sensation, ear whistling, jacket whipping, walking resistance
non_instrument_sensory_compass.parameter: Terrace Microclimate Wind Scour & Evaporative Desiccation
non_instrument_sensory_compass.zero_instrument_procedure: Hold cloth strip at arm length. Observe face and ear wind feel: Light breeze (felt on face, leaves rustle: 5-11 km/h); Moderate breeze (raises dust, small branches move: 20-28 km/h); High gale (large branches sway, walking impeded, ear roar: 39-49 km/h).
non_instrument_sensory_compass.fao_nrcs_interpretation: High mountain winds double transpiration water loss and snap tender cold shoots. Wind speed above walking resistance requires immediate windbreak fencing.
non_instrument_sensory_compass.remedial_action: Erect 1-meter high brushwood or dry-stone baffle on windward terrace crest to create a quiet wind shadow zone equal to 4-5 times wall height.

non_instrument_sensory_compass.standard_authority: NRCS Snowpack Telemetry (SNOTEL) Field Calibration & Permafrost Active Layer
non_instrument_sensory_compass.body_metric: 1st knuckle (~2.5 cm), 2nd knuckle (~5 cm), wrist (~18 cm), elbow (~45 cm)
non_instrument_sensory_compass.parameter: Snow Layer Depth & Thermal Insulation Cover
non_instrument_sensory_compass.zero_instrument_procedure: Plunge open hand with fingers together straight into undisturbed snow cover until fingers contact firm ground or crusted ice layer.
non_instrument_sensory_compass.fao_nrcs_interpretation: Dusting (fingertip): negligible insulation, ground freezes hard. Hand-depth (wrist): protects overwintered roots from deep frost. Forearm deep: substantial thermal insulation; soil underneath remains unfrozen at 0 C.
non_instrument_sensory_compass.remedial_action: Mound cleared snow onto outer wall embankments to act as a thermal windbreak while keeping planting bed cleared for solar warming.
